speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Their contributions, past and present, helped to make us who we are today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: All over the world, women build families and keep families together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women also tend to contribute more to their families if they work and add to their families' financial well-being.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Evidence from a range of countries shows that increasing the share of household income controlled by women, either through their own earnings or transfers, changes spending in ways that benefit children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While this statistic referred more to developing countries, we know from our own experiences that, in Singapore, women play a pivotal role in ensuring the holistic well-being of our families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women create social capital in communities through building strong families, caring for the young and old, and supporting fellow women through job opportunities and networks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women often quietly drive community programmes that benefit residents and rally for resources and help through their own social networks to serve community needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Those of us who have been active on the ground would have seen the aunty-networks and the mommy-networks in action, for instance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: An increase in female labour force participation results in faster economic growth since growth is typically driven by manpower and productivity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The World Economic Forum, in its 2016 Future of Jobs report, noted that "Net job growth and skills instability result in most businesses currently facing major recruitment challenges and talent shortages, a pattern already evident in the results and set to get worse over the next five years." Hence, as Singapore seeks to cultivate new growth engines, we should look to our women as a significant source of untapped talent and entrepreneurial dynamism.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In summary, women help to increase social capital and economic prosperity and contribute to Singapore's long-term success.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore has generally done well in recognising and promoting the aspirations of women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, our laws protect women from violence, harassment and discrimination.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Under the law, women have control over our own bodies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Law enforcement authorities do not turn a blind eye to crimes against women, as they tend to in some countries, but actively investigate and prosecute the perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, we have good healthcare and support systems for women and children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our record of safe births for both mother and child is the best in the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, we are the best country in Asia to be a mother, according to an annual index released by international aid agency Save the Children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, Singapore girls enjoy a world-class education and emerge as confident, knowledgeable women, with our own ideas, opinions and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fourth, we have a modern and vibrant economy, providing more interesting job opportunities for both men and women alike.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should acknowledge these strengths even as we aspire to do better.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, the depressingly low board representation, the dearth of female chief executive officers (CEOs) and lower proportions in certain professions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is not because men are inherently more capable or more driven than women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After all, in our schools, girls perform just as well as boys.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Rather, it is because our society does not fully provide the support that women need to achieve our aspirations in the family, community and workplace at the same time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is why the People's Action Party's (PAP's) Women's Wing put up several position papers over the years, lobbying the Government to take tangible action.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of these recommendations will be reiterated today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Supporting Singapore women to fulfil their familial and career aspirations and to help them to be future-ready require a whole-of-society approach, but it is important that we start in this House.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hope is to take a positive and progressive stance in moving this Motion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women are not asking for special treatment or privileges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Nonetheless, there are pragmatic, concrete steps that the nation can take in various areas to help women to achieve their aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I would also emphasise that many of the recommendations that my colleagues and I are putting forth in this Motion apply to Singaporeans regardless of gender.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our support for women − and men − to balance their multiple roles should help them reach greater heights, in our economy, in various professions, in social work, in the arts and in sports and in many diverse frontiers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our recommendations are organised along four strategies: first, create capacity; second, provide options; third, remove barriers; and fourth, to be future-ready.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I will introduce these areas and describe some specific ideas under each of them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My fellow colleagues who support this Motion will provide further elaboration and explanation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First of all, we need to recognise that most people do not journey through life in a straight line and neither do we assume only one role at any one point in time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is not a simple case of simply going to school, then work and then retire.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Often, we are sons and daughters as well as fathers and mothers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Both men and women do take time out now and then, for our children, parents, school, training and other worthy pursuits.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, while men and women both have to juggle our many obligations at work and at home, women face particular challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women have traditionally been and still are the primary caregivers at home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Being nurturers at heart, it is little wonder why women care so much for our loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But women also have career aspirations, and it is fair for women to want to work and give their best shot at fulfilling their ambitions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our nation and economy also benefit with more women working, as articulated earlier.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With an ageing population, smaller families and evolving expectations, we need to make available adequate care options and strengthen our support for caregivers so that their capacity can be freed up to pursue their careers as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to rethink how the childcare and eldercare facilities are designed and situated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The key consideration must be to ensure availability and easy access to such care facilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To help women to return to work, care facilities for the young and old need to be near workplaces as well so that working women, and men, can quickly respond to emergencies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Retrofitting existing workplaces to accommodate care facilities will take time and will be costly, too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, this concept should be incorporated as a requirement when new parcels of land are sold or when redevelopment is on the cards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One challenge with centre-based care is the limited operating hours of the centres.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In many jobs, workers often need to work overtime or stay back late to deal with emergencies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, could the operating hours of care facilities be extended so that working adults, especially those who have little control over their working hours, can be assured that their children and elderly are safe and cared for?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A complementary measure is to help establish a network of caregivers comprising full-time homemakers or retirees who can help working mothers fetch or take care of their children during times of need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am heartened by the introduction of the Allied Infant Educarer (AIE) initiative this year but these are tied to centres with formal operating hours.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could we help by making available AIEs who have spare capacity outside of centre operating hours?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: An online directory can be created to help match demand with supply.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Interested parents who cannot secure a placement at the infant care or childcare centre can look to this platform for potential caregivers within the neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Basic profile and credential of these caregivers can be published in the directory.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are services already provided for by the Government, but a concerted effort is needed to help women hoping to return to work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In developing the capabilities of women, the courses should aim to refresh existing professional skills; acquire new skills to re-enter the workforce or enter new industries of growth potential; develop entrepreneurial capacity, for example, through e-commerce; and cultivate digital fluency, a point that I will further elaborate later.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Courses should also incorporate modules that help in confidence-building, personal grooming and information technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Next, the package should help those who have acquired new skills and qualifications to embark on a career by matching them to suitable opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some stay-at-home mothers I spoke with agreed that an effective package must take a holistic approach and have tangible follow-ups.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the difference is in whether, after completing the courses, this will lead to real opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And for those who may not immediately secure a job after training, the package could offer a period of internship for employers and potential employees to adjust and ensure better fit of industry needs and skills to get that foot in the door.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such assistance should also apply to men who wish to return to work as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must recognise the aspirations of the younger generation of workers who desire greater work-life balance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They want to be able to give their families and careers their 100%.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As societal norms shift, we also see more fathers and sons sharing the duty of care at home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, making FWA more pervasive benefits all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I understand that it is challenging to apply FWA across all industries and sectors in one broad stroke, because the nature of jobs is not homogenous.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Each standard will specify a set of progressive practices that are verifiable and are also industry- or sector-specific.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Upon meeting the standards, MOM can recognise the employer with an "FWA mark" because standards without audit would be quite futile.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Taken together, laws, guidelines, standards and advisories will form a comprehensive map to help employers build fair and progressive workplaces.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Employers can then make public their adoption of these standards through the Jobs Bank and the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) website.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Jobseekers would then be able to identify these companies as their employers of choice.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One tangible way of encouraging employers to institutionalise FWA is to adapt current standards, schemes and awards, such as the Singapore Quality Class (Niche Business Excellence Standard for People) and TAFEP Exemplary Employer Award, to require fulfilment of FWA standards as a minimum criterion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Employers should also be encouraged to update their appraisal system and criteria.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many employers still appraise employees based on facetime, regardless of the quality of their work produced or the positive peer reviews and customer reviews that they receive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, a holistic approach is needed when implementing industry-specific FWA standards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Another option to enable women to work while caring for their young and old at home is to help them become entrepreneurs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As entrepreneurs, they can stay economically active and have better control of their schedule at the same time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Mastercard Women's Entrepreneurial Index 2016, for instance, ranked Singapore at fifth position, citing strong enabling conditions for womenpreneurs, such as high opportunity to attain advanced knowledge assets and access to mainstream financial services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should take advantage of this and encourage women who wish to take the path of entrepreneurship to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We could also dedicate support to help them set up shop online and link them up with fellow womenpreneurs, so that they can exchange business ideas and opportunities, collaborate in partnerships, and help and mentor one another.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To empower women to achieve meaningful progress, we need to also remove the barriers that constrain women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: An invisible but critical obstacle is how women are being perceived and pigeon-holed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We, therefore, need to challenge the stereotypes of and reshape the attitude towards women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At home, fathers and sons are integral family members and have equal responsibilities in ensuring the well-being of loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government has, in recent years, been signaling the need for shared family responsibilities by increasing paternity leave and shared parental care leave.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These changes also help to correct the perception of women being a greater liability than men at work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On the ground, we have also observed more hands-on fathers and sons.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, things are changing, and we must continue to build on this momentum to encourage a more equal share of care responsibilities at home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women tend to fall off as they progress up the career track.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Surely, we have many more women who have the competence and calibre to sit on boards!

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women also tend to concentrate in certain sectors and roles.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These realities highlight the invisible walls and ceilings that women face.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, we must work to improve women's access to opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is a positive move and an aspiration that is highly achievable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Setting such a 2020 target is certainly not about asking for special treatment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, we should be conscious of our unconscious bias and avoid a biased selection that disadvantages women right from the start.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fourth, be future-ready, having smart women for a smart nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we look to the future and move towards a Smart Nation, we must also embrace technology which is a critical enabler to the above goals.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Digital fluency can help to close the gender gap and level the playing field for women at work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, the digital fluency gap between men and women is one of the largest in Singapore compared to the other countries surveyed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Digital fluency not only opens up new career opportunities for women in the digital age but also enables women to exploit smart solutions that help to create capacity and options.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the right smart solutions, women, and men, can remotely manage situations and monitor their young and old at home while they are at work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Smart solutions can allow women to work productively and respond efficiently even if they have to be away from their offices, thereby enabling flexible work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Technology can also act as a networking tool for women in their aspirational pursuits.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Digital platforms can allow women to exchange useful information and create job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: E-commerce platforms, for example, can help stay-at-home caregivers monetise their skills or overcome resource constraints in starting their businesses and, in the process, maintain financial independence, stay plugged in while continuing to care for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women can also make use of these platforms to raise funds, find mentors and network with other women entrepreneurs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, there is a strong case for cultivating and strengthening digital fluency amongst women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Education in schools builds the digital foundation for our next generation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, today's Motion is unprecedented in the history of this Parliament.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is not a feminist Motion; instead, it hopes to strengthen Singapore's foundation and help Singaporeans, be they men or women, to achieve their full potentials and prepare for our common future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We can all see that Singaporean women have made great contributions towards the family, the society and the country.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In recent years, many studies have shown that women in the labour force can help improve the family's well-being, increase social cohesion and promote economic growth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although Singapore has made outstanding achievements in many areas, women need to catch up in certain aspects of life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Among citizens who have a tertiary education, more than half are women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, capability and motivation are not the main impediment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking at the current situation, it is not difficult for us to guess that women still are the primary caregivers at home, and it is a challenge for them to have spare time and energy to do other things.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are an Asian society, looking after our parents and children is an undeniable duty.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, be they sons or daughters, fathers or mothers, they must carry this duty of caring for one's family equally.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fortunately, more and more fathers and sons are willingly taking up the responsibility to look after the young and old in the family.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition, modern Singaporean women enjoy good education and, naturally, they would have dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, the above does not just apply to women only.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My Parliamentary colleagues and I hope that through this Motion, we can win more concrete support for Singapore women, so that they can fly high and fulfil their family and career aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): Sir, this is the first time this House is debating on a Motion concerning the aspirations of women in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My colleagues and I moved this Motion not to lobby for affirmative action, but to build on the strengths of women, to recognise and close the gaps.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But most importantly, we desire to make Singapore the best home for everyone − a home where regardless of background or gender, Singaporeans have the capability, opportunity and courage to pursue our aspirations and lead a full and happy life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The world we live, work and play in is an exciting one, undergoing unprecedented changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is affecting all industries and jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This digital disruption is changing the landscape not only of work, but also of how work is done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We should take the opportunity to reflect on what this could mean for both men and women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Leveraging digital technology and mobility can make things more accessible and inclusive by enabling FWA and enabling people to work when and wherever they wish to.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There must also be supporting policies and an organisational culture around how work is done and rewarded.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: FWAs must be part of the work culture and how work is done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Otherwise, what it will only serve to do is highlight the differences between men and women in the workforce and may be seen as concessions given to women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: FWAs must be accepted as the way work is done and not special arrangements made for women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For example, collaborating virtually and working anywhere should be and is increasingly becoming a norm for employees and not seen as an exception.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This will allow more effective communications and collaboration for workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Having supporting policies will indirectly encourage and enable men to participate and have a more equal share of the family and duties in the home.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For sustained impact and greater participation and success of women in the workplace, companies and leaders in organisations must also champion the value of tapping the female talent base, developing women for good jobs as well as be committed to tracking progress and retaining women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With female university undergraduates outnumbering male undergraduates in Singapore, women are increasingly likely to be equally or better educated than men.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Two-thirds of the jobs that will be available in 2020, as we all have seen in studies to date, have said that these jobs do not even exist today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What this means is that when we learn, we need to prepare ourselves for careers that may not yet exist.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With growing digitalisation, we need to build new skills and be comfortable with technology to successfully navigate this multifaceted and global environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Technology and engineering skills are growing in importance across industries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Although we are seeing an increasing trend of females opting for Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education in Singapore, women and girls remain significantly under-represented in both education settings for engineering science and IT as well as in the workforce for these fields.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: These are jobs that are expected to have the most growth in the next five years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This would mean that there will be a large portion of our population missing out on critical skills to further their careers and this could mean that they could also risk missing out on the next disruptive trend that could improve Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Minister Vivian Balakrishnan, in his keynote speech at the Internet of Things (IoT) Asia last week, said that "There is a disruption going on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: People are worried about jobs and people are worried about wages.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This is real and no politician can afford to ignore this." He also said that "the most important political challenge is to prepare our people for this revolution." He stressed the need to build the skills and capabilities to enable our people to leverage this digital disruption, thereby generating good jobs with good wages which is at the heart of what a Smart Nation is about.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We need to ensure that girls at a young age are exposed to education, both formal and informal, on digital technologies, with opportunities to have hands-on learning and experiences.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Both the Government and businesses must take an active role and commit resources to attract more women in tertiary education to STEM education and training.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: These could include scholarships, internships and career coaching.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We must set goals to increase the number of women in technology roles and take action and track the progress.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Many will agree that, in Singapore, we have made good progress in the workforce participation of women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And this should be attributed to more accessible and quality childcare as well as the introduction of the family care and paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But we should not just track the percentage of women in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We must also look at how women are doing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But I must stress that this is fourth in the world, which is a very strong achievement.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: To achieve gender pay parity, employers should make it a point to understand and address the gap and pay for comparable work done by both men and women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I think the Government should also focus on ensuring and encouraging employers to do that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This is above the average among countries in the Asia Pacific region, shown in the survey by global consultancy firm, Grant Thornton.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But if we look into the numbers across C-Suite positions, this has been falling for that same group, meaning, for CEOs, chief financial officers (CFOs) and chief operating officers (COOs), the numbers have dropped from 2016 to 2017.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This is timely as, despite a highly educated female population, greater workforce participation by women and an increasing proportion of women in senior business leadership roles above the average amongst countries even in the Asia Pacific region, not enough attention is paid to those rules.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What we are seeing is slow progress for women in senior leadership positions in C-Suite positions as well as on boards.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And we have to ask ourselves why this is so, in order to come up with the right actions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Possible areas for change criteria would apply around decision-making principles for selection and the expansion of networks or talent pools that organisations are sourcing for board talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Beyond mentoring and cultivating the pipeline of women for boards, we should be putting women in the roles that build the skills and experiences required for board roles, including C-Suite positions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Unless women have the relevant leadership and scope of business leadership experience, even if we dictate a number, even if we set a goal, that is not going to happen unless we allow women to get the experiences that they require to qualify for the board positions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: To prepare women for board positions, we should also be deliberate in efforts to support women in senior business roles to develop for these roles.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can executive leadership education programmes to equip senior leaders with board skills be included as part of their eligible courses for SkillsFuture Credit?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This will allow women in senior business roles to take ownership of their training for skills required of board members.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I believe that this is one of the factors that is causing the slow progress of women in senior leadership roles as well as in participation on boards despite a highly educated women talent base and a pipeline of women in senior business roles in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Some of us may think that we are not.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Unconscious biases are pervasive in most societies and often people are unaware of our own unconscious biases.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: So, although this is going to be quite embarrassing for me, I thought I would just share a personal story and an "Aha!" moment that I had to illustrate the point about unconscious biases.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Sometime last year, I had a very important client meeting, and we were preparing for speakers for that meeting and my colleague assured me that we had the best speakers lined up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We had one topic on quantum computing, a fairly exciting and interesting topic but requiring a good amount of knowledge and skills to be able to explain that well and to cover the topic well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Of course, I was looking around for the speaker and then I realised who the speaker was, so I turned to my colleague and said, "Are you sure you did your homework?" And he said, "Yes." I said, "Are you sure?" And I was not quite sure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Anyway, the speaker spoke and for the next one hour, I was extremely engaged, inspired and the speaker did a very good job.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I was totally embarrassed after that because it was an "Aha!" moment for me because I had just completed my unconscious bias training, and that is why it made an impact on me of my own unconscious bias because, guess what?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The reason why I thought she was not the best speaker for this, is not because she was a female, but it was because she looked young and she was also extremely good looking.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And I said to myself, "Gosh!" this is extremely embarrassing, because I do pride myself on feeling fairly open and I am a champion of diversity in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But it was not her gender; it was age and my assumption of experience and know-how at the same time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I think if I look at all the statistics and the facts that are supporting us in having female talent in key positions, clearly, something is blocking that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We need to boldly ask ourselves why and face that and be able then to do something about it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I would recommend that we have training for unconscious biases both in schools and in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I am passionate about having more women in both public and private organisations, because it makes perfect business sense and social and economic sense when you consider that women make up 50% of our population.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Globally, they represent a growth market more than twice the size of China and India combined.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: So, it will take both men and women to make the difference and enable us all to do our best work and to be our aspirations, both men and women.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of the Motion because I hope to see more measures to enable our women to achieve their aspirations and reach their fullest potential.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although Singapore women have similar opportunities for education, training and work as men, our society still expects them to fulfill their traditional roles as mothers, daughters and daughters-in-law.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a result, women continue to shoulder the bulk of housework and caregiving duties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even if their workloads are as demanding as those of their husbands', women are expected to take care of domestic affairs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In many cases, when it becomes too difficult to meet both the demands of work and home, women would always put their families first, sacrifice themselves and take a step down their career ladders or stop working.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Personally, I would like to see greater support and recognition of the caregiving and nurturing role of stay-at-home mothers, and also greater empowerment for those who choose to contribute in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With an ageing population, we can expect to see even more women shouldering caregiving responsibilities for parents, in-laws and relatives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our women are a precious resource and should be fully supported in their careers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To remain competitive as a nation, we need to secure the contribution of every qualified man and woman in our labour force.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For families to be able to entrust the important responsibility of caregiving to professionals, we should continue to seek to boost the capability and capacity of our professional caregiving sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The current system can be enhanced such that, upon retirement, retired nurses can give consent to sharing their contact details for future re-engagement opportunities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would help to alleviate the shortage of healthcare workers and at the same time the community can continue to benefit from their wealth of experience.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They can also, through the course of their work, share tips on how they can take care of their family members better.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Building up this network of retired medical professionals will complement what the community can offer.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, by augmenting our professional caregiving sector, we will help women stay in the workforce while providing them and their family members peace of mind, knowing that their elderly family members are being taken care of.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must continue to step up the recruitment and training of manpower for the caregiving sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This group of professionals will play an important role in enabling the females in our labour force to achieve a higher participation rate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would be very much appreciated for family emergencies involving the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As I had said during the Budget Debate, many of them do not have much savings and would hesitate to ask for money from their husbands or children to attend classes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By helping them with the costs of the courses, we will enable more women to pick up skills and return to work more quickly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These monthly transfers will provide acknowledgement and greater long-term financial assurance and is a meaningful way of recognising the great value of all the unpaid work and services that homemakers render to nurture their children and care for their parents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last but not least, I appeal to the Government to treat a single mother and her children as a "family nucleus" for Housing and Development Board (HDB) applications.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Single parents face enormous struggles caring and providing for children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should help them by providing a stable and safe environment for the children to grow up in.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Accommodation is a basic necessity to ensure the safety and well-being of vulnerable children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Research has shown that stress in children has a negative impact on their developing brains, "with consequences, including cognitive deficits and emotional disorders, which, in turn, help perpetuate disadvantage." It is very unhealthy for these disadvantaged children to have to stay in overcrowded homes of their parents' friends or relatives, where they may not feel that they truly belong or embarrassed at having to do so.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the very least, with a roof over their heads, mothers will have one less worry and be able to focus more of their energies on their work to finance the expenses of the families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, supporting and empowering our women will enable them to contribute more to their families, communities and country, and achieve their full potential.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With women holding up half the sky, supporting the aspirations of our women is the most effective way to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, for some of our Singapore women, building successful careers and closely-knit families, are closely intertwined.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Their aspirations are inextricably linked by a relationship of trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some find that the demands of work prevent them from settling down earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Others, while they enjoy parenthood, find balancing work and family a struggle and hope for better support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Still for others, the demands of motherhood and career meant the decision is binary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These trade-offs are difficult to make because, for most people, careers and families define us to a large extent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While it is unlikely that we can have our cake and eat it, can we do better for our Singaporean women?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The need to find careers, success and financial stability before marriage is probably a significant reason for this phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The knock-on effect of later marriages is having children later.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) treatment, such as in vitro fertilization (IVF) is increasingly being used by couples.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The reduced subsidies rate commensurates with the lowered chances which are graduated after 40 years old to 42 years old, and not a precipitous decline.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, we need to review expanding the subsidised options for our couples.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, there are approximately 14 certified AR doctors in the restructured hospitals and about 33 in private practice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Opening up subsidies to both public and private hospitals give our couples more options and shorter waiting time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For couples with narrower windows, time is of the essence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The worry that doctors in private practice will raise prices because of the subsidies is not trivial.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we have similarly been using a system of audits and checks for community healthcare subsidies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The AR fees are now comparable between the private and public sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And the smaller group of AR practitioners meant checks should be easier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Opening up the market also introduces greater contestability for competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The issue of AR is less critical if a woman marries earlier and have children earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are unlikely to reverse the trend of later marriages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we can give women chances of giving birth to healthy babies even when they are older.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The hon Member Miss Cheng Li Hui raised in 2016 if the Ministry of Health (MOH) can consider allowing for egg-freezing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A key consideration then was whether egg-freezing was effective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to a Straits Times report on 18 September 2016, "In 2012, the American Society for Reproductive Medicine removed the 'experimental' label from egg freezing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It found that advances in techniques led to pregnancy rates comparable to IVF cycles that use fresh eggs." Even in IVF, eggs are extracted and then frozen before thawing for fertilisation, although for a shorter period of time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the same report, it said, "Doctors note that a woman is born with a finite number of eggs, with the number and quality of eggs declining as she ages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By age 40, she has only 3% of the up to two million eggs that she was born with.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This was from a study by the University of St Andrews and the University of Edinburgh.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Hence, freezing the eggs at a younger age preserves her fertility." Now, the concern that allowing for egg-freezing might delay marriage and parenthood is also not trivial.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, sourcing for donor eggs is already allowed in Singapore anyway.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And for many women, it is not just a matter of work delaying marriage but finding Mr Right.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should grant our women that right to choose without denying them the option of having healthier children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can, in fact, support the aspirations of our Singaporean women by giving them a better chance of raising healthy children and having a good career.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Turning to the workplace, many women with children find their career options limited by inflexible workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The recently-announced initiatives by the Government on the pilot in the Civil Service and Standard Chartered's 20 weeks of paid maternity leave are clarion calls to help our mothers manage their balancing act better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Standard Chartered stated it had done so because it "recognise  the dual roles many of them have to play and want them to succeed both at work and at home." And we need more of such trailblazers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that the Government can consider piloting the right to request for FWA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, after giving birth, many women need some time to get used to managing the dual roles of childcare and work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For many new mothers, the first year after childbirth can be exhausting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They hope that their work can be flexible so that they can better cope with the role of a mother.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, they also realise that they already have the 16-week maternity leave and asking for FWA might affect their career prospect.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While success and recognition are not only the defining factors of what every woman aspires to have, many women do find satisfaction and a sense of achievement when they can manage a good balance between their careers and families.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In Singapore, with equal access to quality education and jobs, we have seen a rise in the labour force participation rate (LFPR) of women.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But with an ageing population, human capital remains one of our most valuable resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, it is worth looking at what more we can do to encourage more women in returning to the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From various focus group discussions, many women attributed their challenges in returning to the workforce to three things.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One, education system; two, Asian culture with an overbearing societal behaviour and mindset that caregiving is primarily women's responsibility; three, weak transition support back to the workforce First, on education.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is a broad topic and we know it is important.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But what level of emphasis we place on our future generation matters.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: After a generation, the school curricula have significantly changed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Today, many parents in their 30s and 40s found that they are unable to provide homework guidance to their children in school unless they are also trained in the same methodology that is being taught in school.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Additionally, there seems to be an unspoken assumption that children will or should have external tuition classes if they are unable to catch up in classes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How much truth this assumption holds remains to be proven.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But an obvious trend is the extensive amount of tuition classes that our Singapore students have to undertake in order to cope with the daily homework assigned, much less the hope to excel in the subject or the sport that they desire.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some blame the universal top-down education system that expects the students of different capability to learn at the same pace being unrealistic.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Others claim this is the result of the school not teaching sufficiently.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Another camp laments that this is the result of poor resource distribution in public schools and teachers having an enormous burden to cope with many aspects apart from teaching.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Whatever the reason may be, it has certainly created an industry in its own right − tuition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Those who can afford or have aced it with the help of tuition would say there is nothing wrong with this trend.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: After all, it is one of demand and supply.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, there are larger implicating issues we must deliberate on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Has this created more stress on our parents in thinking that having tuition is a prerequisite and without which their children cannot keep up at school?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Will this lead to higher cost of raising children and less quality time for the family?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will provide some relief for school teachers, more accessibility to families that have lesser means and also to focus the tuition only for those who really need it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It not only drives our choices but, more importantly, the culture of a society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We have increasingly seen younger Singaporeans who are willing to take the unbeaten path to pursue their dreams.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we encourage more entrepreneurs, their success depends largely on whether they are passionate, resourceful, have the grit to overcome the challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But before that, will we have a supportive culture that enables them to succeed, a culture that accepts failures as part of business endeavours and embraces different definitions of success?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I think that is what we look forward to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Next, let me raise six areas in which I think we can continue to advance women's representation in the workforce while we continue to encourage procreation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We must recognise that these efforts cannot be solely achieved through advocacy unless all parties involved take concrete steps towards the same goal.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, continuous improvement in company policies and human resource (HR) practices.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we have heard from the previous few speakers, FWAs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To me, this is not a terminology that can be implemented without trust and adjustments to the work processes and also a company culture.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Employers and employees have mutual roles to play in understanding the issues at hand and jointly build the mutual trust that is required in a working relationship over a long period of time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Employers, who traditionally feel that the physical presence of the employees are critical in an office as it relates to effective work time, should progressively take a different view of this.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They have to empower and equip their staff to work and deliver in different contexts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Likewise, the employees must demonstrate a strong ownership in delivering results and effective work and time management to give their employers adequate assurance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This would help alleviate our manpower crunch and provide vocational opportunities for women who are keen to continue actively contributing in our workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some multinational companies (MNCs) have male champions who advocate the cause and actually give recognition to fathers for playing an equal and prominent role in supporting their wives at work and also at home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In such situations, when both parents are able to strike a balance and achieve well at their work, and find their work meaningful, they are likely to strike a better balance and remain involved in their children's lives and in raising their children together to strengthen their family units.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Further, unfair employment practices are still observed unfortunately in terms of salary and benefits that discriminate both gender and age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Without a clear signal on fair hiring, progress in this area will continue to remain slow and many part-time jobs remain unattractive despite the fact that some of our older workers will gain financial independence.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, targeted SkillsFuture package for those who plan to return to the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Women who had extended breaks from work during childbearing years need assistance to return to the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Having left the working environment, they become unfamiliar with what it feels like to be back in the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Their self-perception of their own abilities and also what relevant work skills they may have, are lacking and this will prevent them from wanting to return to the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I encourage SkillsFuture SG to consider having a structured programme that does two things.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One, provide a tailored skills training or courses that are relevant to areas for workers who have been out of the workforce for more than two years, for example, in confidence-building and the IT-related courses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is very critical, whether it is through our Place and Train Programme or even the Adapt and Grow schemes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There are some women who have left the workforce for a while.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They have found that they have passion in new areas and they hope to switch careers after they have delivered.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And I think they need to embark on this career switch that will better suit their capabilities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With these, women will be kept relevant professionally and they have confidence that they are also well supported in their career development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Empowering women to pursue careers in which they can balance their family life and continue contributing to the economy, in the long run will only be a positive move.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will ensure that during their old age they will also have some amount of financial independence.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Encourage our companies and the public sector to have mentoring programmes for promising female employees as they progress in their career.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Mentorship enables women to understand and also share their challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They need to have a ready network to confide in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And above all, an aspirational motivation, when they see that other similar females have achieved in life and they are also equally capable of achieving those goals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: During the Committee of Supply (COS) this year, I have raised about the need for preventive care and community caregiving as there is a limit to the number of elderly care centres that we can build and we hope to enable our elderly to succeed in ageing successfully at home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the responsibility of caring for the elderly falling on the shoulders of a smaller pool of individuals, we need to provide and encourage more options for caregiving.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I feel that caregivers should be given courses on how and what it takes to care for the elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I have asked this at the COS and I will raise it again: whether the Ministry will consider providing these family caregivers the basic options of training on how to do caregiving for the elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Also, whether the Ministry can work with healthcare providers to develop an information kit of proven digital gadgets that can be installed at home so that the caregivers are better facilitated to take care of their elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And are there any application platforms that can be created to link the caregivers with sources of help provision or even for them to be networked with retired medical professionals to supplement the healthcare sector?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On subsidies and care leave, there are two areas I recommend be reviewed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, for non-working mothers − the current subsidies that the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) has for infant care, childcare or kindergarten for these non-working mothers are actually lower compared to those of working mothers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As the duty of caring for the elderly still primarily falls on the children, for those who are singles or come from a single child family, they would face even more difficulties with the weaker support.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Fifth, provide enhanced support networks for single parents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We spoke about this extensively during the COS this year.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For single parents, such networks and extended support are very critical as many would have fewer choices and even less help available.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Assistance and support from counsellors, volunteers and having the knowledge of where to access this information are very critical.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With such support, they will be better equipped to manage their time and financial resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Their children would also benefit from adults who can act as mentors like bigger brothers or sisters to them, whom they can turn to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For example, in Korea, where the startup scene is more vibrant, women are actually more involved in the customer service-oriented and consumer industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One possibility is to convert the heartland shops to house such entrepreneurial businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Micro-franchise concepts like social enterprises should also be considered, especially if they can provide the vocational opportunities for the elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And next, availability of shared platforms for local entrepreneurs to create an industry of their own.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: All these services that are offered would provide the flexibility not only for the worker but because it can be catered on demand.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With proximity and also reliable supply of services, this can help ease the burdens of working parents who cannot afford to have FWAs or who have to work on shifts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To end off, Mr Deputy Speaker, women's aspirations can only be effectively fulfilled with the support of our broader society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As much as women want to continue working to be active contributors for as long as they could, their dreams cannot be fulfilled on their own.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The society has to embrace and support their journey.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There is always that X factor that makes or breaks a dream.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I hope Singapore continues to be progressive and lead the way to push our boundaries for shared and equal responsibilities among every Singaporean − men or women.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And with this, I rise in support of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But, like Sylvia, the eight male members of the Workers' Party (WP) in the Chamber today wish to affirm our strong support for the aspirations of Singapore women.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I think, at present, they hold up even more than half.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Women bear the lion's share of homemaking and childcare in our families.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are, for the most part, the most critical role models for our children during their precious formative years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their care and their example shape the quality of the next generation of Singaporeans, thus setting the tone and the course for the future of this country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But all too often, Singapore women become the stressed tuition teacher-in-chief, fielding incessant almost day-to-day communications with their children's school administrators and teachers, coaching the kids in the evening, managing tuition classes, ferrying children to and from these classes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore mothers are at the frontlines of an academic system that places a huge burden of academic content mastery on our children while layering ever more non-academic demands on top.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Women also still bear the brunt of keeping the home clean − our homes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Women who work very often have to cook and clean after they return home from work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans put in among the longest working hours in the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The norm of long working hours, which does not equate with high impact if productivity is low, places many women in the hardest of positions: stay longer at work and have to work at housekeeping and coaching children till late into the night, sacrificing sleep and health, or leave the workplace early and risk their promotion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, Singapore women are at the frontlines, this time of the issues of productivity and long working hours that Singapore is grappling with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In saying that, I do not downplay the contributions of the small number of stay-at-home fathers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nor do I want to downplay the role of the many, many husbands and fathers who play their part, a meaningful part in raising the children and keeping the home clean.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But on the whole, Singapore men are no different from men all over the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can and they should do more in the home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Men can do more to be with their children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can do more to guide their children's academic and character development.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can do more to form strong, close, trusting relationships with their children, relationships that will last till the end of our lives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For our children are among our most important companions in life's journey.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those relationships should be an immensely important part of what make a meaningful life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And those relationships are the touchstones of emotional stability, self-mastery and character, for both parents and children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For me, being a part of my children's lives as they are growing up has been not only emotionally rewarding but has been a huge source of wisdom and learning.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Men can do more to keep the home clean.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Domestic helpers play their part, but they can only do so much and they are another category of women who need to be treated with respect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And most Singaporeans do not employ domestic helpers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Machines like the "irobot" floor cleaner can only do so much.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whatever work that is left over needs to be shared more equally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, men can and should do more.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the cornerstone of men doing more is to respect women as equal human beings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When that respect is practised beyond lip service and words but in day-to-day actions and thoughts, that respect will inevitably spill over to all social institutions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That respect will help eliminate the vestiges of inequality that women still face inside and outside our homes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Social norms are created every single day by our behaviour as individuals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to reflect on those behaviours which include our speech and our habits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No one should refer to a grown woman as a "girl" any more than we refer to grown men as "boys." More can be done by our companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a growing body of research that shows that gender diversity is not only correlated with better business performance but that there may be an actual causal connection between the two.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Companies can, for example, promote mentorship programmes for older and more senior female employees to coach and counsel younger female employees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some professions tend to be dominated by women, like teaching, social work and nursing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More can be done in these professions to attract men and create male role models so that these industries, too, will gain the benefits of gender diversity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And finally, the state plays a huge role and a much bigger role in Singapore than in most developed countries relative to civil society and the private sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The role of the state in Singapore is crucial in fostering the kind of gender equality of opportunity, choice and respect that should characterise Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there more that the state can do?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this is still a small number and I suspect that even more civil servants would take this option if there was better assurance that career prospects would not be set back from a spell of part-time work and that it is easy to transition back to full-time work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore's Civil Service is not only Singapore's biggest employer but an employer that often sets labour market norms by the power of its example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having more civil servants on part-time and job sharing would set a powerful example to the private sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could, in turn, enable more women to join the workforce and also exit and re-enter more easily.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The state should also step up efforts to root out discrimination based on gender, alongside any other kind of unworthy discrimination on anything other than performance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The time has come to regularly survey and publish perceptions of discrimination and seek to find patterns that can be addressed by MOM and TAFEP to ensure a fair workplace.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a society, we are mature enough to have these conversations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The state can do more to facilitate women re-entering the workforce.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOM could work with the Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) in various industries to allow homemakers to keep abreast of industry developments and attend ad hoc events and training, through email, newsletters and other online resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would better prepare women who choose to re-enter the workforce at some point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The state should also catalyse mentorship programmes for women in large companies, as I referred to earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A good place to start would be the Civil Service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Ministry of Education (MOE) consider a structured system for inviting women from different professions to give talks at our schools about what they have accomplished?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Role models make a huge difference in life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Female students need more tangible examples that whatever obstacles they face in their future workplace can be overcome.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sexist attitudes can be formed and hardened during National Service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By the same token, National Service can be a powerful platform to reinforce positive ideas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) organise talks and programmes to educate National Servicemen about the evils of domestic violence and sexual harassment?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, if women hold up more than half the sky, a single parent, man or woman, is holding together the entire world for their family.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time for us to stop brushing aside this idea with the broom of the moral hazard argument.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hardly anyone chooses to become a single parent as a lifestyle choice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Granting equal benefits will not provoke a rash of people wanting to become single parents, with all the financial and emotional challenges that that entails.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once we recognise just how outrageous this idea is, we start to see that there are no sound objections to equalising benefits to single parents and thus not punishing their children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the aspirations of Singapore women that we will be affirming and advancing?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a man, I am in no position to speak for women.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I can only share my view, which is that Singapore women should have what all human beings should have − choices, the choice to strike the balance they want to in the workplace and in the home; the choice to strive and achieve their dreams in any line of work they apply themselves to; the choice to be an amazing homemaker who enables her family to fulfil their deep potential and, in so doing, enables herself to do the same.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To make Singapore a home where all women have these choices, we need institutional equality of opportunity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Here, the state and private sector can and should do more.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need men to step up and play a greater role in the home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And most of all, we need to continually reinforce that glue that binds men and women together in families, in the community and as a nation, and that glue is, quite simply, respect.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, what are the aspirations of Singapore women?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many would want to be a caring mother, loving wife, filial daughter and dutiful daughter-in-law, plus a successful career woman.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To be very honest, women are, in general, still shouldering more family care responsibilities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, FWAs, or flexi-work, will be especially important to their careers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The recent Conditions of Employment survey showed some improvement in the number of workers who can access flexi-work, especially ad hoc flexi-work, like unplanned time-off and ad hoc teleworking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But worryingly, the momentum seems to have slackened.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The proportion of firms offering formal flexi-work, like flexible hours and working from home, has not increased.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, in the United States (US), around 45% of the working population works from home.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have also heard that the tendency is for employers to offer flexi-work to older workers, particularly to those holding lower positions, whose work they feel are more dispensable or less important to the company.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But flexi-work is essential to everyone, especially young parents who are juggling the care of children or those who are taking care of aged parents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government look into the profile of workers with flexi-work and see if we can do more to expand it?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many firms do not offer long-term flexi-work because they are scared it will affect their productivity or they do not trust their staff.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are afraid "working from home" will turn into "shirking from home".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But studies show that this is not the case.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They worked longer hours but, simultaneously, were happier.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Specifically, firms can retain more female talent with flexi-work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, many women choose to leave the workforce when they cannot balance work and family responsibilities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When more people in the family have flexi-work options, they can also help out with family responsibilities more, so that the women do not have to leave the workforce altogether.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The lack of flexi-work is part of a bigger problem, which is the culture of facetime in local offices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some bosses like to see employees spending long hours at their desks, even if studies show that such employees are not more productive.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If flexi-work takes off, then bosses will have to adapt to a culture where they do not see their employees at their desks for long hours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They will learn to assess employees only on their work, not on the amount of facetime.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hopefully, this will help even employees who do not take up flexi-work to cut down on unproductive facetime.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope employers will seriously relook at their operations and HR practices to accommodate more flexi-work.
