speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, when there is more flexi-work, it may also encourage more married couples to have more children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, when I talked to my younger residents, they told me that the Government has given them a lot of monetary incentives.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They said, unfortunately, it will not sway their decision.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They said that every day, they have to rush from their workplace to childcare centres to pick up their children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And that process, that journey itself, is always very stressful because they have to rush.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just now I talked about women who are in the workforce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many full-time homemakers do not have adequate CPF savings, even though women live longer than men and need even more retirement savings.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are two main ways to address this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, to encourage lifelong learning and paths back into the workforce for younger homemakers, so that they can re-enter the workforce when they want to.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Give them more SkillsFuture credits or enable the transfer of unused credits from family members.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sourcing for more effective e-learning courses and putting them in the list of courses applicable for SkillsFuture subsidies would make them more accessible for homemakers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the Budget allows, the Government can give dollar-for-dollar matching, up to a certain maximum sum.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Inertia will ensure that a significant amount gets transferred to these women, who have given their whole lives to build their families and country.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Allow me to summarise in Chinese.here1 (In Mandarin):   What do Singaporean women want?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think most women want to be a loving wife, a caring mother, a filial daughter, a dutiful daughter-in-law and a successful career woman.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Honestly speaking, in most Singaporean families, family responsibilities fall mostly on the women.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, in order to achieve these goals, FWA is very critical.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: According to the latest statistics, the percentage of companies that offer FWA seems to have hit a bottleneck.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, it is because many companies feel that with FWA, their staff will become lazy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, studies have shown that staff who are on FWA not only have higher productivity but are also less likely to resign.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Government to study how to encourage companies to offer more types of FWAs and longer periods of FWAs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: FWAs should not only be offered to low-income workers, but also to all the staff.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should study how to change the mindset of local employers and let them know that a good employee is not necessarily someone who stays in the office every day.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, we should not neglect women who have left the workforce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should encourage housewives to undergo lifelong learning and give them opportunities to go back to the workforce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For some housewives, not having enough CPF savings is a big problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although family members can opt out, I believe this will benefit quite a number of housewives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, one of Singapore's founding principles is the creation of an egalitarian society that is based on meritocracy and justice.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Everyone, regardless of race, language, religion or gender, has an equal place in our society and we, as a nation, have been progressive in supporting diversity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Women in Singapore have made, and continue to make, steady progress over the years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In business, we find more women in senior management roles.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the Development Bank of Singapore (DBS), for example, a third of its group executive committee is female, and, in Singtel, women made up one third of its board of directors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, although she is not currently in the Chair, the fact that our Speaker is addressed as "Madam," is a testament to this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While women in Singapore continue to make advancements in their career advancement, we must remain cognisant that the playing field is sometimes not level for women.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Gender parity can be achieved only if we make a conscious effort to foster an environment that facilitates opportunities and mobility for women, and I will speak on three areas that I think will help bring us closer to parity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, how to enhance the working and corporate environment for women.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Gender diversity at workplaces today is one of the top of mind concerns for companies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although women, in general, have made good career advancements at work, the number of women in senior leadership roles is still far lower than that of men.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And that was mentioned by Member Ms Jessica Tan in her speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my opinion, this can be attributed to at least two plausible reasons.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, biasness might have unconsciously crept into organisational processes, such as performance evaluation and even promotion decisions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Organisations, have in recent years, put in place many pro-family policies to support flexi and part-time work, as well as Women Initiatives Networks (WIN) to raise awareness around gender issues at work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The results of these policies, however, are mixed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not uncommon to hear anecdotal stories of how women and men are evaluated using different yardsticks, and this is especially so when women take on flexi-work or during the period when they go on maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel that the way that we appraise and evaluate employees for promotion must also change.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The adoption of electronic work platforms, such as project management software and collaboration platforms, will enhance the ability of women to work from home and allow them to make equal contributions at work regardless of whether they are physically present in the office or not.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Companies, both in the public and private sectors, should accelerate the pace that these technologies are adopted and help their organisations to move towards a flexible workforce where both women and, indeed, men as well can continue to contribute to the company's success, regardless of whether they are working from home or working on-the-go.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can also do more to help and support families and couples holistically; this is my second point.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the biggest hurdles that working mothers face is the need to juggle both work and home responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This challenge stems from the fact that societies, especially those in Asia, tend to ascribe gender-specific roles to men and women.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Men are typically assumed to be the primary breadwinner and women's careers are thought to be of secondary importance to men's.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These attitudes have led to the "sacrifice" mindset that is common among both men and women where women are often expected to "sacrifice" their career goals and aspirations to support their family, so that their husbands can pursue their careers wholeheartedly and undistracted.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite the voluntary career slowdown, it has not been easy for these working moms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They often have to work three shifts a day − a day shift in office as an employee, an evening mommy or wife shift where they need to fulfil their family responsibilities, and a night shift where they would check their emails and prepare for the next day's work after they have gone through homework with their kids and put the kids to bed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most of the corporate solutions that we have to support working moms tend to revolve around FWAs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this is useful, I believe it is clearly insufficient because we need to also support working dads so that they can be empowered to support their wives with the family responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that the support for working dads can come on three fronts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, how can companies adopt a pro-family mindset and implement progressive HR practices that support both men and women, so that they can better fulfil their family obligations without fear that they will be penalised at work or worry about their career being derailed?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, from a policy perspective, what can the Government do to facilitate working dads who wish to take on more family responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we provide more support for men who decide, for example, to be stay-home dads?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, as a society, we need to collectively destigmatise stay-home dads and see stay-home dads as fulfilling just as important a duty as stay-home moms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Individuals, companies and the Government must celebrate and recognise the contributions of mothers and fathers, regardless of whether they chose to work or to stay at home because they are fulfilling an important and sacred duty that deserves our collective and unwavering support.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My final point, Deputy Speaker, Sir, is doing more to help full-time homemaking moms return to the workforce in either a part-time or full time capacity and calibrating this with the SkillsFuture initiative.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we try to move towards a manpower-lean workforce that relies on technology to boost our employees' productivity, we will inevitably face a skills-gap issue, especially among full-time moms who wish to return to work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the present climate, back-to-work moms already find it difficult to reintegrate back to the workforce because they might have lost the business networks that they used to have, and they have to deal with the fact that what they knew is obsolete.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This problem is compounded by the adoption of workplace technology that back-to-work moms could be unfamiliar with.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to help our back-to-work moms transit smoothly back into the workforce by ensuring that they have the right level of skills and knowledge to reintegrate into the labour market.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we even have more credit for the stay-at-home moms who are willing to return to the workforce either in a part-time or full-time capacity?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And other than ensuring that back-to-work moms must have market relevant skills, job matching market placement is also crucial.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I have said before that everything I am today, I owe to four amazing women: my grandmother, my mother, my wife and my sister.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What inspires me to continue to make our society a more inclusive and gender equal one is the fifth amazing woman in my life, my five-year-old daughter Kelly Anne.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want Kelly Anne to grow up in a society where she has more positive female role-models like our all-women Everest team, top corporate leader Olivia Lum, Senior Assistant Commissioner of Police Zuraidah Abdullah and the Republic of Singapore Air Force fighter pilot Khoo Teh Lynn.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want her to grow up in an environment that will empower her to be successful both in her career and in her family life, without having to compromise either.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want her to grow up feeling proud to be a Singaporean woman and proud because she lives in a country that provides her with multiple opportunities for success, regardless of race, language, religion or gender.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Sir, I conclude my speech in firm support of the Motion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: First and foremost, I would like to thank Ms Tin Pei Ling and the Members for raising the need to recognise and support Singapore women, many of whom have made personal sacrifices to care for their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: It is an important responsibility, which will only grow heavier with Singapore's ageing population.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The Government is strengthening efforts in a number of areas so that caregivers feel more supported in caring for their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: First, we are enhancing accessibility to eldercare services in the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We are building our eldercare centres across Singapore and ramping up transport services so that it is more convenient for seniors to travel to the centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: New centres will operate minimally from 7.00 am to 7.00 pm so that it is more convenient for working caregivers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We are also encouraging more centres to extend their operating hours and establishing home care services at their centres to make care more accessible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We will need more manpower to support this expansion and are enhancing schemes, such as the Return to Nursing scheme, which aims to attract retired and home practising nurses to return to work in the healthcare sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We also have Professional Conversion Programmes to attract mid-career Singaporeans to be trained as nurses and allied health professionals and organise job fairs as well as put in place the Community Care Traineeship Programme to attract Singaporeans to be trained as support care staff for the aged care sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Second, we are expanding our respite services so that caregivers can rest and recharge and working caregivers can travel for overseas trips.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Other than weekend respite services at our eldercare centres, more than 40 nursing homes now provide residential respite services ranging from a few days to a month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Caregivers of seniors with dementia can also tap on the Eldersit and Home-Based Intervention Programme which offers home-based respite aimed at keeping the seniors engaged in activities in a familiar environment while their caregivers take a break.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Caregivers co-pay as little as $10 after taking into account training subsidies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: To date, more than 35,000 caregivers have utilised the grant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: In October last year, we started piloting an eldercare training scheme for our FDWs to better care for seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: These FDWs undergo a comprehensive training before deployment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: As of last month, about 60 FDWs have been trained, of which 50 have been placed with families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Fourth, we are increasing the touchpoints in the community to help caregivers navigate the social and healthcare systems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: In 2014, we launched the Singapore Silver Line which is a one-stop call centre to help seniors and their caregivers with information on care services and schemes in the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) has also set up AICareLinks centres at five hospitals and at its office in Maxwell Road.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: These are one-stop counters where caregivers can receive advice on services and schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: To facilitate easier access to information, AIC will set up information booths at selected polyclinics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We now have booths in three polyclinics at Chua Chu Kang, Marine Parade and Yishun.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: AIC will roll this out to another six polyclinics by early next year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Many Members suggested that employers provide FWAs to allow employees to better manage work demands with family and caregiving needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: In 2016, about 67% of the employees worked in firms that offer formal FWAs, up from 56% in 2011.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: More than eight in 10 employees worked in firms that offer unplanned time-off or ad hoc teleworking for their employees to attend to personal matters, up from seven in 10 in 2011.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan has suggested that the public sector take the lead in enabling FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We agree with the suggestion and would like to update the House that all our public healthcare clusters have done so to help staff balance work and personal demands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: For instance, more than 4,200 nurses are benefiting from FWAs, such as having more flexible rosters enabled by e-scheduling systems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan and Ms Joan Pereira also suggested to provide more eldercare leave for working caregivers to take care of the seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Existing leave provisions can be used for this purpose today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We encourage more employers to provide family-related leave benefits which can be used for different purposes, as well as FWAs, such as time-off to look after their elderly parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Public Service agencies currently provide two days of parent care leave annually.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: This would include caregivers who are singles and taking care of their elderly parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We will continue to review the need to legislate eldercare leave as our socio-economic circumstances change over time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling suggested to leverage technology for remote monitoring of our seniors while caregivers are at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: As part of HDB's Smart Homes Trial, we are testing elderly monitoring systems which can send out alerts to their caregivers if the seniors are in distress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: This will allow caregivers greater peace of mind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: For example, in Yuhua, residents can install solutions, such as the Smart Elderly Monitoring and Alert System (SEMAS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The system can provide alerts to caregivers when the seniors trigger the distress buttons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: It can also send automated notifications if the system detects an anomaly in the seniors' behaviour, such as lack of movement over a prolonged duration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Ultimately, supporting our caregivers is a collective responsibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We need to build a community support system where our seniors and their caregivers are supported and cared for.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Under the Community Networks for Seniors pilot programme, we are partnering community stakeholders to reach out, befriend and support seniors living in each community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We are also promoting dementia-friendly communities by encouraging the community-at-large to be trained to help seniors with dementia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: In these "dementia-friendly communities", seniors with dementia can stay active and caregivers do not have to be afraid of them going out, because there will be people around to help them home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Together, we hope to foster a more inclusive and compassionate society where caregivers are well-supported in their caregiving roles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The Government will also continue to study new ways to support our caregivers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We agree with Mr Desmond Choo that we need to support women's aspiration to raise healthy children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: There is sufficient capacity at ART facilities in our public hospitals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Clinical data in Singapore also shows that public and private centres' success rates are comparable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Nevertheless, couples seeking treatment at private ART centres may tap on their MediSave to defray the cost of ART treatment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: On egg freezing, licensed Assisted Reproduction (AR) centres in Singapore are allowed to do this when there are medical needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: For example, egg freezing can be performed on women who need to undergo medical treatment, such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy, that may adversely affect their fertility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We would also like to highlight that egg freezing carries some risks to the woman.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The process of stimulating production and collecting a woman's eggs for freezing can result in complications, such as over-stimulation of the ovaries, bleeding and infection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: In addition, the issue of allowing egg freezing for non-medical or social reasons is a complex one due to various ethical and social implications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: First, egg freezing is not a guaranteed solution to delaying parenthood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Second, the risks of developing certain age-related complications during pregnancies are not mitigated by egg freezing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: For this reason, the Government still encourages couples to have more children when they are relatively young and healthy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We are weighing the social, ethical and religious concerns very carefully.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Should social egg freezing be allowed, we will need to build a robust regulatory framework with adequate controls not just to ensure the safety and welfare of the women undergoing social egg freezing, but to also mitigate the potential social, ethical and religious considerations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Through various measures, we hope that women can be better supported to fulfil their aspirations as well as their many essential roles in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I agree with the thrust of what Ms Tin Pei Ling and Members who have taken to the floor before me have said, that we have a duty to support women in their individual aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have made great strides towards gender equality over the years, but much can be done.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2016, literacy rate for women is at 95% and that for males is close to 99%.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This gap, I believe, will disappear in several years' time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, from my generation onwards, there is practically no education gap between men and women.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And as mentioned by Ms Tin Pei Ling and Ms Jessica Tan, female undergraduates make up the majority of students in university.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, it has been so for the last five years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Women now are also well represented in lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Of all Singaporeans who utilised their SkillsFuture Credit last year, 55% were women.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Despite this, there is room to grow and to further narrow the gap between men and women, and one area for us to do so is the gap in employment rate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A key reason is because the employment rate for women shows a drop after the 25-29 age bracket when many start their families and never quite return to match the participation rate of men.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Similarly, while the wage differential between men and women is narrowing, and the rate of income growth for women has outpaced that for men over the past five years, there is still a significant wage disparity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think it depends on whether we include CPF and whether the employer's CPF is included.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What then should we do to further close the gap?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many helpful suggestions have been raised, such as skills training, job matching services, encouraging freelance work, financial support and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to recognise that there are challenges unique to back-to-work women.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While mindsets may be slowly shifting, there remain significant societal and familial expectations of women to be the ones to take care of the household, look after young children or elderly parents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As they seek to return to work, they will need more understanding and support to help them juggle or move between their various roles in the family, community and at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They may have been out of the workforce for some time while caring for their families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of them may want to take the opportunity to start their careers afresh in a different industry and will need advice and support.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some may be out of touch with the latest technology or developments in the industries they were from and, hence, they lack confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to address these unique challenges, even while we tap on programmes and assistance that are generally available to all workers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the process of planning and implementing this initiative, we will build in a plan to reach out to back-to-work women.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can have outreach and engagement workshops specifically catered to back-to-work women, to engender peer support and address emotional, psychological and other issues that they face.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will point them towards the key programmes that will assist them in their return to the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this regard, I think several Members have raised the possibility of a package of programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, having 18,000 SkillsFuture Credit-approved programmes in our directory is overwhelming.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For certain segments, we need to draw out what are the few 10, 20, 50 programmes that may be especially useful for them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of these, for example, IT programmes, as suggested by Ms Jessica Tan, can be part of this package.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For others, such as back-to-work women who used to hold more senior positions, this can include programmes to help prepare them to sit on boards, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And still others who have been out of work for a few years and may be lacking in confidence, we can point them towards programmes, such as those on employability skills, that can help them regain their confidence or meet other people in the same shoes and have the peer support.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, such employability programmes are what the tripartite partners have been doing for some time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I think it will be quite a big package.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But there are two points I would like to specifically mention.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, a few Members − I think Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and also Mr Darryl David − have talked about giving more SkillsFuture Credits to women in this position.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We went through the COS debate where I went to great lengths explaining support from the supply end and support from the demand end.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SkillsFuture Credit is a support from the demand end.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last year, we spent about $40 million supporting SkillsFuture Credit.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But on the supply end − this is when we support and fund programmes to lower their course fees to make them accessible − we funded $400 million worth of subsidies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, $40 million SkillsFuture Credit and $400 million on programmes at the supply end.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the situation of a back-to-work woman, we should make use of the subsidies and assistance on the supply end where the focus is much sharper to help them enter industries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, that is one area I would like to point out.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second area I would like to point out is that most of our programmes are actually well-subsidised and accessible to all, regardless of gender, a point emphatically made by Ms Tin Pei Ling earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a skill that many of us − young and old, men and women, employed and unemployed − need to pick up.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It may not be helpful to have a special programme for any specific segment which may give the impression that it is a deficiency faced by this particular segment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Likewise, in organising job placement services, I always have a preference for inclusive job fairs that cater to everybody.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then employers who participate are more likely to be open-minded to all segments of jobseekers − young workers, mature workers, retrenched professionals, managers and executives (PMEs), back-to-work women, ex-offenders and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And then we will have a higher chance to ensure a better job fit for both employer and employee.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Having said that, I keep a totally open mind and I will consider whatever is most effective in ensuring that vulnerable workers can gain the right skills and gain jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we must be mindful that we have a broad range of training programmes and interventions at our disposal.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can customise in one of two ways.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I suggest that we also offer guidance and support to let women decide on their own customised line of courses and training.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If I were to draw an analogy, it is like YouTube.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: YouTube is an inclusive depository of videos catering to all demographics and all segments in all kinds of interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But based on your searches and interests, it recommends you the videos that might interest you.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is no YouTube for one segment and YouTube for another segment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is only one YouTube but different searches.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we customise our assistance on the searching process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As with many outreach programmes, it is always the last mile that is the most important.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Together, I am confident that we will be able to build the scaffold for women to pursue their aspirations in a more equal society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I stand in full support for this Motion put up by Ms Tin Pei Ling and the other Members of the House.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There has been much ongoing debate about women's rights all over the world and through the decades.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Women have been held back from full and equal participation in their societies because of narrow definitions of gender roles that have not evolved with the times.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Even today, the global movement for women's rights and gender equality continues the struggle to make progress.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we have, indeed, made some progress.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We can be proud of our own notable women politicians, such as Chan Choy Siong, an activist for women's rights who was key to the creation of the Women's Charter, and Dr Kanwaljit Soin, the first female NMP.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Today, young girls − just like young boys − must attend school, because of our longstanding commitment to compulsory education.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Clearly, their importance as economic contributors of this country cannot be under-estimated.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Because of these achievements, there are people who believe that gender equality is no longer an issue here.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yale Prof Deborah Rhodes described this as the "no-problem problem", that is, the erroneous perception that the problem of women's rights has been solved because there is evidence of growing opportunities for women.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The fact is, women continue to be constrained by discriminatory attitudes and practices, preventing them from participating in public life as full equals.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let that figure sink in − 117 years.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the last two general elections, female candidates for Parliament faced sexist scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: An example to demonstrate the pervasiveness of this bias is this: a newspaper introducing several candidates on the same day, described three men in its headlines as "banking executive, engineer and professor", while a woman entrepreneur became "mother of two".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Being a mother is undeniably very important and deserves recognition.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, putting women in the same frame implies that women only belong at home and are defined only by their family.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Now, some may say that these choices of words are merely turns of phrases by the media.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our language reflects our socio-cultural mores, attitudes and relationships.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How we describe women has a direct impact on how gender relations are socially constructed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When we resort to terminology about gender stereotypes, we entrench these same stereotypes into society; in short, we normalise them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The media play a crucial part in promoting positive gender roles and eradicating gender stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We should not assume that gender stereotypes will automatically go away over time.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One survey from AWARE spoke to over 1,300 respondents.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, 58% of men in this age group believed that women should take care of household chores and caregiving, compared to only 38% of women.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It seems that young women have much more equitable views than young men.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What are we going to do to inculcate fairer and more progressive views in young men and not just in young women?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We often hear of "traditional values" being passed down from one generation to the next.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These "values", however, are often rooted in patriarchal constructs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And despite most family units now being dual-income ones, there remains an inequality of roles in housekeeping and caregiving, which women are expected to take charge of.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, because many families engage foreign female domestic help, men are further excused from doing household chores or tending to their children or elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There is also an unwillingness to let go of these "traditional values" because they are "how things are meant to be", or they are "natural".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They are how things have always been, as dictated by religious and cultural beliefs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is in the "nature" of men to be breadwinners and head of households, and of women to bear and raise children.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I work in Drama Box Ltd, a theatre company, and I am the only man in this company.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The rest, all seven of them, are very capable women.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: At this moment, all the seven women are in Rotterdam, as the company has been invited to participate in the International Community Arts Festival, showcasing our work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Leading the team is a woman, Associate Artistic Director Koh Hui Ling and then, at the same time, she brought along her young toddler, three-year-old Eunice, with her.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And the rest of the team would be there to help her to take care of Eunice whenever she is busy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And then, I wonder how many of us men here, who travel a lot, would bring our toddlers along?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There is, of course, no biological or behavioural science that can back up the assumption of gender stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Nobody "naturally" knows how to operate a washing machine, soothe a cranky newborn or help an elderly relative take medication at the correct time, or clean and shower them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These activities, like many, many others, transcend gender.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But the sad fact is, we educate girls and boys very differently, with gender stereotyping already taking place at the earliest age.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Little boys are told how strong they are and little girls are told how sweet they are.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They are told stories where their whole lives and fates are bound up in their gender, instead of being allowed to develop as individuals.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard anecdotes from a parent, who shared that her child's preschool teacher had bought presents at the end of the school term.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The boys in the class received books about superheroes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The girls received presents, too − books on how to become a princess.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How can we change the education system, so that every child, whatever their gender, can develop in the way that is best for them?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Can our pedagogical materials explicitly include gender equality, rather than imply stereotypes and biases, both wittingly and otherwise?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We see this sort of reductive stereotyping in state policy- and decision-making as well.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the lifetime income and CPF accumulation of women are lower than that of men − despite women having longer lifespans.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This means women actually have a higher risk of experiencing poverty at old age than men.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In a greying society like Singapore, this, in itself, should be cause for great concern.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Greater strides must be made to bridge this gender divide to ensure the well-being of our female citizens.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These policies reflect the gender stereotype that childcare belongs to women.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This reinforces the idea that women can, and should, "choose" to "focus on the family", as opposed to furthering their careers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, it entrenches a discriminatory attitude that rationalises income disparity between men and women, hiring policies and even promotion prospects.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is it any wonder then that Singapore's female labour force participation rate is lower than that of countries of similar income levels?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One of the markers of a first world nation is gender equality and, by that, I mean equality not just in economic terms, but also in social ones.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In our efforts to galvanise national economic growth, how can we better harness the potential of over 50% of our population?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Statistics from MOM show that women still earn less than men, never mind that they have the same working hours and qualifications.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How can we strive towards parity, so that we can reward our best workers according to achievements, rather than their gender?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We celebrate when women are appointed to new positions of leadership – the first female Speaker of Parliament, Madam, the first female full Minister.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We call this "historical", using phrases like "big strides for women".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As it stands, only 24% of people in Parliament are women.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some say it is better than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But equality should not be granted based on time.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It should be expected right here and right now.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A society that truly embraces gender equality is one that offers protection from harm towards men and women alike.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, today, we allow for contentious legislation that permits domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How can we turn a blind eye towards a brutal act of violence like rape simply because it is committed by a family member?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How can we, as a society, or as policymakers, protect vulnerable members of our society?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our conversation has not even begun to address the rights of the transgender community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It may be an uncomfortable topic for some but, nevertheless, an urgent one.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our stand as leaders and our actions as lawmakers impact how society views and treats the transgender community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The more we talk about these issues, the more embracing and positive we are about their rights, the better they will be treated in school, at work and in their own families.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I bring this up because, at some point, we should go beyond gender altogether and just look at human rights the rights of all humans, the equality of all humans.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As a forward-looking society, we must take active steps towards a strategy of "gender mainstreaming".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This term, established by the United Nations (UN), as a strategy for promoting gender equality, involves "ensuring that gender perspectives and attention to the goal of gender equality are central to all activities − policy development, research, advocacy/dialogue, legislation, resource allocation, planning, implementation and monitoring of programmes and projects." In short, the state must take on a proactive approach in establishing policies, be they in terms of education, employment or social welfare that promotes a mindset shift towards gender equality.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, we not only strengthen our economy, but also ensure that we help citizens, regardless of gender, to achieve their aspirations, develop a positive sense of self-worth, as well as ensure their long-term well-being.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We, as policymakers, must advocate for change and take firm steps to eliminate this discrimination for the betterment of our nation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Virginia Woolf wrote this thought-provoking line in chapter 1 of A Room of One's Own, "Call me Mary Beton, call me Mary Seton, call me Mary Carmichael or any other names you, please.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, women have many different identities, multiple voices and perspectives and cannot be seen only through work, one lens.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the same way, we men have to do that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We have different identities and we can assume many, many different roles.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then, we have a much more enriched human experience.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Here, a woman has access to education, healthcare and can make various choices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The fact that we have this opportunity today to speak about the aspirations of Singapore women, and are joined by the men, is a telling sign of our progress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The reality, though, even in a country like Singapore, is that there is much still left to be done to improve the situation for women.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I was fortunate to have been involved in the drafting of the PAP Women's Wing paper issued in July last year and would like to share some insights.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As we looked at some research and reviewed the milestones in a woman's life, we observed that various life circumstances lead women to make significant decisions and commitments which impact on her current and future financial well-being.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, as highlighted by several Members, women tend to be the primary caregivers for their family members.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If she is working and she has children, there will, inevitably, be some impact on her career as she takes some time away for child birth, recovery and caring for the child.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She would have to decide on the commitment she puts into her work versus the time she would spend with the child.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There may also be those who fall into the category of vulnerable women because of unfortunate life events like divorced women with children and single mothers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We also see that the current generation of retired elderly women tend to depend on their spouses and children for financial sustenance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The fact is that women generally live longer than men and may outlive her spouse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The children tend to have their own financial commitments.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, some women may not be able to retire and need to continue working to earn income to sustain their expenses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Yes, we have seen many women overcome these challenges and do well to balance their career and family life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The reality though is that various life circumstances result in many women being unable to fully exploit career opportunities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This takes a toll on her ability to work towards financial well-being and building her nest egg.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Further, if a woman decides to stay home to care for her family, she should not be penalised and be financially disadvantaged because the work she does at home is equally significant to what she does in the office.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important for us, therefore, to look at certain measures to safeguard a woman's financial well-being and improve her retirement adequacy in the long run.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Financial education should be institutionalised and implemented as a core life skill to students.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, we should look at embracing this life skill in MOE's 21st Century Competencies and integrate this into the teaching of other subjects, with increasing levels of sophistication as our students progress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a slew of financial planning courses, mostly for adults.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: MoneySENSE is a good platform and its efforts should be developed further.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Outreach needs to be enhanced and more collaboration should be developed to implement more target-specific programmes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Further, adding to the wish list for SkillsFuture, I believe we should also use the SkillsFuture platform to create intensive and meaningful financial literacy programmes which can help people plan their finances throughout life and to navigate difficult times.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that there are already top-up schemes in place and, in this regard, I support the proposal made by Er Dr Lee Bee Wah yesterday.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This would nudge women to work towards a target and, hopefully, develop a saving habit.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In reviewing this, we should also look at how to further encourage and incentivise family members to recognise the efforts of unpaid caregivers or homemakers who are not in the workforce and to help them build on their retirement monies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I echo the sentiments made by other Members and note that Minister Ong Ye Kung had yesterday touched on this in his speech.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Typical situations we see are of homemakers whose children have grown up or long-term caregivers whose loved ones have passed on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Recognition should be given to their experience in long-term caregiving, household management and related skillsets.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Back-to-work preparatory, conversion or certification programmes should be developed to help them monetise their skills and meet the national demands for caregivers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Women in Singapore today are fortunate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Life in our country is so much better, compared to life in the past and in other countries.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our rights are protected and we have many choices to improve our lives and the lives of our families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, women must possess a sense of self-responsibility, the motivation to continue improving their capabilities and be informed about programmes and assistance that are available, as well as of opportunities to upgrade themselves.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On this matter, one aspect that I feel we should pay attention to is the financial situation of a woman and her retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The ups and downs in a woman's life often compel her to make decisions that will have an impact on her financial situation, not only in the short-term, but also for the long run.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can also find elderly women who are dependent on her husbands and children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The situation is quite worrying, especially if their husbands are no longer around and their children cannot afford to take care of their elderly mother.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, I feel that it is important that we try to increase awareness and put in place certain mechanisms to safeguard the financial health of women in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Amongst other things, I have proposed that financial education begins at an early age.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The principle and awareness on the importance of taking care of our financial health should be inculcated in schools.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These are the things that I feel can help improve a woman's financial situation as well as her retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, what is more important is a woman's awareness and desire to continue improving and to take care of herself so that she will not suffer when she faces challenges or when she is in her golden years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A woman who has confidence and skills will improve the lives of her family and the community around her.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, I am very privileged to have this opportunity to speak in this House, before you, a woman Speaker, and be amongst intelligent and inspiring women and men, doing our best to lend our voices to those whom we represent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have made much progress in supporting the aspirations of Singapore women over the years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should continue in this effort so that women, regardless of their age, family circumstances and challenges, may continue to contribute towards the development of this nation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: "Any woman who understands the problems of running a home will be nearer to understanding the problems of running a country." These were words uttered in 1979 on the campaign trail by the late Margaret Thatcher, a trail that led to her election as Prime Minister of the UK and a trail that she then blazed as The Iron Lady.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The actress Meryl Streep who played The Iron Lady summed up her legacy as "(having) given women and girls around the world reason to supplant fantasies of just being princesses with a different dream: the real-life option and possibility of leading their nation; this was ground-breaking and admirable." The immediate past Secretary-General of the United Nations, Mr Ban Ki-Moon, said recently that, "Countries with higher levels of gender equality have higher economic growth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Companies with more women on their boards have higher returns.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Peace agreements that include women are also more successful.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Parliaments with more women take up a wider range of issues, including health, education, anti-discrimination and child support." In our own local political sphere, we have many more women actively participating and contributing to the growth of our nation in recent years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can and should have more in this august Chamber, but we are getting there.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Outside of this Chamber, the world is changing as well, but perhaps not as fast as we should.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We live in a world almost evenly split between men and women, but women worldwide have been fighting for equal rights, equal opportunities and equal pay for long, and yet, regrettably, their efforts have yet to bear abundant fruit in many countries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even China, India and Hong Kong register a healthier growth in this index.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And our female board members get less than half the remuneration of their male counterparts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, it should sadden us that half of our population are not getting their just dues.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They know what they want − as chief executives, as businesswomen, working women and also not forgetting some as homemakers and mothers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They aspire for the best and will not stop at anything lesser than that.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this House we have many capable and inspirational women, talented in different fields and, in the course of the debate on this worthy Motion, much will be said about and suggested on how we can achieve better gender parity on corporate boards as we journey towards achieving the aspirations of Singapore women.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, I shall not attempt to make a weak attempt at claiming to have any solutions that are better than those already put on the table.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Instead, I hope to raise three related points that need to be said amidst this debate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we work on the top end of the ladder, strengthening the diversity of talent at the mid-level and also open doors at the entry level, we must not forget that there is one group that has decided not to be on the ladder, either temporarily or permanently.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are our stay-at-home mothers as well as family caregivers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some make conscious decisions to take on a role that they feel very passionate about; others, perhaps through circumstance, have had to take on the roles and also put their hearts into being the best in their unique areas and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their roles are, therefore, no less important in society, but the challenges that they face are also no less worthy of our solutions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many make sacrifices on income, healthcare, personal aspirations, all so that those they are closest to can either have a good start or a comfortable end.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are a society today that is fast consumed by productivity and even our policies towards women are somewhat driven by that same desire.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thus, it is unfortunate that it appears that a working mother seemingly becomes more highly valued than a stay-at-home-mother or caregiver.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not easy for working mothers and they should rightfully be supported.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the converse, that stay-at-home-mothers or caregivers have it easier, is a fallacy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we can all acknowledge that mothers in general have an important role to play in their children's development, so why should mothers be differentiated between those who are working and those who are not?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have come to the realisation that fathers, too, play an important role in parenting and we have made moves for fathers to be more involved.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But again, if we do not make a distinction for them, why skew it for women?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To encourage this, I urge MOM to consider raising the interest rate returns for voluntary top-ups and increase the CPF Cash Top-up relief from spouse to spouse, or from child to parent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There have been suggestions for a mandatory system of contributions but I think we should encourage a voluntary system first.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thirdly, for those who wish to return to the workforce when their children are older or when their caregiving roles have evolved, then they should be provided sufficient support to reintegrate them into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It does not have to be only about re-entry into full employment as the transition can sometimes be very difficult.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Promoting more flexi-work arrangements, part-time work, targeted at stay-at-home-mothers and returning caregivers, will make the transition easier.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even as we urge for greater meritocracy so that women have better representation in the workplace and leadership positions and in society, what is perhaps missing in the statistical equation at the moment is that we do not have a lot of concrete studies on current perception of gender equality in Singapore, especially amongst younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the maelstrom of information out there, the UN Human Development Report ranks Singapore at the top in Asia for gender equality in 2015.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, we are also one of the worst performing when it comes to gender equality in the boardroom.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While there is not a lot of available perception surveys for young Singaporeans, the just released findings of the Gender and Millennials Symposium on Gender Equality perhaps is telling.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Prof David Cotter and Dr Joanna Peppin looked at 40 years of gender surveys and since the 1990s, 17- to 18-year-olds have overwhelmingly endorsed the idea that men and women should be equal at work and in politics − 90% and higher − that is, 17- to 18-years-olds believed that gender equality is important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, the same study found that the idea of gender equality at home had conversely slipped.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, addressing this perception gap is an important step towards better understanding of gender equality.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There needs to be better studies on gender perceptions in Singapore because this will allow us to make better decisions and also address the root causes of the lack of gender equality at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And perhaps also educate younger Singaporeans on the importance of gender equality.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On a lighter note, the last point I wish to make is that we also need to acknowledge that stereotypes do not just affect women.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When we fight gender stereotypes levelled against women, we also need to be conscious that we do not end up confirming male stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We move rightfully away from the perception that women are not the weaker sex.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think it is important for us to also realise that men are often boxed into needing to appear to be tough, to always have no emotions, to be stoic and always not express their feelings.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Former US First Lady, Eleanor Roosevelt famously remarked, "A woman is like a tea bag − you cannot tell how strong she is until you put her in hot water." Today, we have showned that women are strong and can rise to the challenge and excel above even men.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Men on the other hand should be free to express their feelings and not just feelings of hunger!

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, we, both men and women, must ensure the aspirations of Singapore women, as well as men, should be met.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Madam, in discussing the Motion that is being tabled, that is, "Aspirations of Singapore Women", various integrated and collective efforts must be made to support Singapore women in achieving these aspirations.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government, community, family and every individual must play their respective roles.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They are both the caregivers and the breadwinners.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The difficulties faced by single mothers should receive concern from all quarters, including the Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Government policies should be more directed towards alleviating the burden shouldered by this group.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is a very encouraging change and is well-received by Singaporeans who are very concerned about single mothers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I hope that these policy changes made last year do not end there but instead represent an initial step for the Government to continue helping this group.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A home is one of the basic requirements for every person.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The lack of a proper dwelling will affect the quality of life and human development as well as the family's development.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They are only eligible to buy a house under the "single" scheme, which has an age limit of 35 years and above.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They are also not allowed to rent a flat under the Public Rental Scheme based on the same reason, that is, their children are not regarded as part of a family nucleus.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Lamentations of "misfortunes seldom come alone" are often heard amongst these single mothers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Not only do they have to bear mental and emotional stress while undergoing divorce and being abandoned by their husbands, they now have to strive relentlessly to fulfil their responsibilities as their family's caregivers and breadwinners.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Stranded in these situations, single mothers should not be further burdened with difficulties to seek out proper and affordable homes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I shall not belabour this point as I believe that the HDB is aware of it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many hope that this criterion will be revoked and exemptions given to single mothers who have gone through divorce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is also hoped that HDB will outline policies that are more inclined to help and empower single mothers in their efforts to meet their basic living needs, that is, a conducive and affordable home, especially while they and their children struggle through this challenging time.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A more positive support from HDB will enable single mothers to fulfil their familial and career aspirations.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I will share this perspective based on my experience as a family and marriage counsellor and also as a husband.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The values that should be inculcated in order to achieve such a family comprises mutual respect, trust in one another and understanding.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These values have to be nurtured, practised and instilled within a family.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In facing a hectic and challenging life, couples must be prepared to help one another in bringing up their children, household chores and also personal development, for instance, pursuing further education, as well as advancement in their respective careers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Married couples, especially husbands as the head of the household, should fashion themselves as a counselling and motivational expert to their spouses so that they will be able to provide moral, emotional and spiritual support and be the motivator for their partners to strive with perseverance and confidence.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such husbands will help their wives become more motivated and positive in balancing and fulfilling their familial and career aspirations.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My question is, when will Singapore take a similar step?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a Singapore Muslim, a husband as well as a father to a daughter, I appeal to the Government to make into reality this call for inclusiveness that is often heard in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My hope is that the Government will reconsider the Muslim community's request for Singapore Muslim women to be given the chance to fulfil their career aspirations and, at the same time, meet their religious obligations.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If the pillars are strong, so will be the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And if the pillars are weak, so, too, the nation." Madam, a country where family, social and cultural values, as well as Government policies are inclined towards empowering women, will produce a nation strong in every aspect − family, social and economy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
