text: In Singapore, human capital is our mainstay in attracting foreign investment and growing our economy in this first world era.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Given that female enrolment at local Polytechnics is 89% of male enrolment and at university level for first degree is at 95% of male enrolment, the Government has been spending almost an equal amount on educating our young women as our young men.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is critical that investment in our people see good returns, that is, having its people remain in the workforce, remain economically active and contributing to civil society.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I think it has been quite well-established that, given a choice, women want to have a career and still be able to fulfil their roles as caregivers in the family.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has done much in supporting working parents through the Baby Bonus package, which comprehensively includes parental tax rebates, parental leave and cash support.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of paternity leave is a bold step in the right direction in inculcating the culture of shared parenting.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, more can and needs to be done to level the playing field for women.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Until we have a pervasive family- and women-friendly work culture, two groups of women need to be supported if we are serious about tapping on the 40% of women who are currently out of the workforce − the working women in danger of dropping out of the workforce due to family-care reasons and the women who would like to return to the workforce after a period of intensive caregiving.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to do more creatively to enable women to remain at work.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Now, I touch on flexible work arrangements to support women in the workforce as well as women returnees.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to decisively plug the leak of experience out of Singapore's labour market by enabling women to remain in the workforce.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This can be done through the implementation of flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Flexible work arrangements are becoming an increasingly viable option for both businesses as well as employees as we move into the digital age and grow our pool of knowledge workers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With more workers in professional, managers and executives (PME) roles, job-sharing, where one full role is shared among two to three employees, is a viable role especially suited for PMEs who wish to scale up on their family-care roles while their children are young.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Young working parents, especially mothers, can still have a meaningful career and contribute to the economy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On a lighter note, the last point I wish to make is that we also need to acknowledge that stereotypes do not just affect women.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: When we fight gender stereotypes levelled against women, we also need to be conscious that we do not end up confirming male stereotypes while nurturing our young.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, employers have been reluctant to offer such options, citing increased manpower costs when taking into consideration the whole salary package, for example, employees' insurance costs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Until they experience the tangible benefits of retaining their female talents, there will be inertia to move.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is more than Work Pro that is provided for FWAs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Other than stopping the leak of experience, such flexible work arrangements, like job-sharing, can also attract women back into the workforce.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: After spending some time away from the labour market for family care, these women may want to step up gradually to help their families as well as themselves transit back into the working world.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If the women can work in meaningful part-time or job-sharing roles, they will have more opportunity to reskill or update their skills while contributing economically.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to support women to return to work.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: At the end of the returnship period, employers may choose to offer these women a position in the company and the women can decide if they would like to be part of the company.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: FWAs should not be seen as a privilege or entitlement for working women, but for all employees with responsibilities and aspirations outside of work.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps it is timely for MOE to look into incorporating education on gender equality and shared caregiving between genders.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: At the heart of the unlevel playing field is the issue of unequal caregiving roles between genders.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that men can also rise to the occasion if they were properly nurtured into the role and given the right support.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially important as our population ages and more working adults are called to provide caregiving to their elderly.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Whether parenting or eldercare, it cannot be seen as a woman's job just because we are good at it.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Setting targets to enable more women to take on leadership roles is equally important.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at the lack of progress in getting women on board, I would urge the Government to adopt the recommendation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Equally important is how we can adopt similar target-setting at different levels of the career ladder.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is to ensure that we will have a continuous stream of women talent being nurtured at different levels of leadership so that we will not be at a loss while finding women directors to make up 20% of the board.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, do you have a clarification?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I listened to Mr Faisal Manap's heartfelt speech.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As a fellow Singaporean, I would like to understand his views better and learn more.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I was wondering whether Mr Faisal Manap feels that the tudung issue is the most important issue faced by women in the Muslim community today, in particular, whether it is a very significant and most important issue.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am hoping I could learn more about the Workers' Party's views and Mr Faisal Manap's views as well.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: First, I would like to answer his point on my personal view.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is important because only in unity do we find strength.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am heartened that our men, too, have stood up to help lend their voice in support of this Motion, which is a positive and forward-looking Motion.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The speeches affirm the importance of the role of women in our multi-racial society and our economy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is a far, far different cry from what we have heard maybe 50 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They gave many practical suggestions to the Government on how to support all women in Singapore comprehensively: in leadership and social impact, employment and entrepreneurship, family and caregiving and financial well-being.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, I find the approach of Mr Faisal Manap worrisome.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: He has used this Motion, which is focused on the aspirations of all women in Singapore, to raise again the issue of the tudung, to focus on differences instead of rallying people to be united.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: He dwells on issues that can injure or hurt the feelings of the community rather than to inspire them.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In fact, Mr Faisal Manap has used many occasions to raise potentially discordant issues in this House.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I sat listening to him many times, championing divisive issues many times, like the need for halal kitchens in our naval ships and his perceived discrimination of the Malays in the army.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Is it his or his party's position that these issues are the top concerns of the community?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There are real socio-economic problems we have to deal with in our community − education, housing, jobs.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Faisal Manap spent some time on these issues but he does not fail to leave behind a semblance, trails of these divisive issues relating to the community, everything from halal kitchens on ships to the issue of Palestine.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: He leaves behind to linger in the minds of our community not only to make them feel different, even to make them feel unjustifiably treated unequally.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Government has responded to Mr Faisal Manap's queries on the tudung issue and other issues, and I will not elaborate today, except to emphasise that we are a multiracial society.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And we all have a role to play to enlarge our common space.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is not to say that religious aspirations are not important.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In fact, they must never be set aside.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Religion is, indeed, important to many of us.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I assure Members that I, too, want to see progress on the tudung issue and religious matters that are dear to Muslims.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am also a father of a daughter.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The process entails understanding workplace requirements and operational needs in the wider scheme of things.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I caution the Member against making this a state-versus-religion issue.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: All these years, our approach has been to win people over slowly but surely, through mutual exchange and meaningful interaction to help Singaporeans understand one another, to understand every community's aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We do this in the spirit of mutual respect, recognising that other communities, too, come with their own perspectives on how they want to live in these common spaces.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Likewise, the community can trust the Government and Muslim leaders to work together on the matter of the tudung.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The community and its religious leaders know that this is a religious matter best resolved and progressed naturally with the acceptance of our larger society.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our religious leaders do not choose to be strident on this matter.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I wonder why the Member chooses to be so.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The issues of Malays in the SAF, tudung, even halal kitchen that the Member has talked about, are not issues of religion only.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Even if they are put up that way, they are difficult issues to resolve.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But, clearly, the way to make progress is gradually and quietly, working under the radar, to strengthen mutual trust and understanding among Singaporeans, so that we can move forward step by step.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, that is how we have got here.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It will only raise the temperature and actually make the problems harder to solve.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Many of us, I understand and I believe, do not support the strident way to solve our problems.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, even on the Internet, I have read about people who criticise Mr Faisal Manap for the way he has taken matters forward.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, there are people who support Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I saw a posting where he was posing at the "Wear White" campaign with Mr Zulfikar Shariff, who was arrested for his views and support for the ISIS terrorists in 2016, I think, for the "Wear White" campaign.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It makes us wonder if Mr Faisal Manap is supporting Mr Zulfikar or is Mr Zulfikar supporting Mr Faisal Manap, or are they in together because of a common cause?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But, indeed, are there common causes they are in together?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Many Members have spoken on this Motion and focused on how well we have done.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our women have achieved aspirations in education, supporting women at work and taking care of their families.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These are things the Government will consider carefully, seriously.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And these are matters all of us must work very hard on.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There is a lot of work to be done but we have made steady progress.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: She is the Commander of the Training Command.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Prior to this, she served as the Director in the Family Education and Support Division and Office for Women's Development, also took care of probation, family issues before she joined MENDAKI.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And let me not forget to mention yourself, Speaker, who has done so well.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are very proud of you, the community is very proud of you.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: You also led NTUC as the Deputy Secretary-General.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: My point is that I choose to use Parliament as a platform, an official platform as an elected Member, to voice out the community's concerns.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I did not choose or post any kind of comment, negative comment, on social media, even though I have my own Facebook page but I did not choose to do that because I know such matters are better discussed officially.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, I believe that as a Member of Parliament, elected through the GRC system, I do have the right to voice the concern.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Some of the concerns that I have voiced out, for example, the halal kitchen issue, was not initiated by me but was mentioned by Minister for Defence Dr Ng Eng Hen.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I was just reiterating what he had mentioned and asked him for clarification on whether there would be effort made to address that issue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: As for the point that the Minister made on Zulfikar, I was there to support the "Wear White" movement.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I just want to repeat one more time: I was there to support the "Wear White" movement.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I am not so sure what is behind Minister's mind when he tried to link me to Zulfikar.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I am a bit distraught by his effort to paint me negatively when what I was trying to do was to voice out the concerns of the community on an official platform and avoid myself from being entangled in this kind of discussion on the social media platform.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, I believe that I have explained enough and I would appreciate if the Minister would be more positive in his remarks towards me.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: He insists his strident approach is the correct way to do what he wants to do, he needs to do.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: What we say about our religious rights, what we say is our right to do things in this multi-racial context may appease a part of our community, maybe it is even because we have to carry it out as a religious responsibility to voice it out.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Member may have spoken in Malay but everyone else understands the translated version, Members in this House and, later on, maybe he is posting to say that "I spoke about this".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But I want to quote what the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Singapore told TODAY newspaper.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: He said, "Religious teachers must be aware that they are not just addressing their believers but also the world as well, and what they say can be heard by others, so they must be more cautious not to be seen as slighting other religions." This may not be about slighting religions but it also stirs emotions within our community and other communities who also have things and rites and rituals that they may want to do but may not be able to do because we value our common space.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, I believe this applies to all of us, all political leaders, when we raise issues on religion or race or language.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In Singapore, we have allowed large doses of freedom in our religious practices, especially those that do not impinge on others.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But when we have to do something that is in the common spaces when we are working together, what we do as what we call our religious rights sometimes have push backs, uncomfortable feelings about what we do, by other communities, and we must recognise this.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, if each community pushes its own claims aggressively, there will be pushback, there will be animosity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Can we imagine that here we are campaigning for our Muslim ladies to put on their tudung, what are employers thinking?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Do we also compromise the equal opportunity that these employers would have employed them on the basis of their competence, on the basis of their ability, and now they have to also consider whether they should be allowed other religious rights that they claim to be theirs?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Thankfully, all of us, most of us, are patient and rational voices and, unlike Mr Faisal Manap, I do not believe things like this should be discussed openly, publicly and then left hanging without answers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I believe that we should call for constructive engagements like he said.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But we must not do it at a place that upsets social harmony.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must not do it among people who have other agendas who we may not be able to control and then may have consequences we never thought about.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I think if we put diary entries today, we would say "nothing of import happened today".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But not so in 1950 when the Court awarded custody of Maria Hertogh against the wishes of the Muslims who consequently rioted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This calm that we have today is not, I believe, the level-headedness of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It leaves a lingering feeling of unsolved, unsolvable and impatience that, one day, I believe, will explode.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: It is the Malay language, it is the national language and it is my mother tongue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I am proud to use my national language in my speech.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: What I have been asking since I was elected in this House is for the Government to address the issue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I called for a committee to be formed, a commission to be formed to look into the concerns of the Malay community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I have not imposed any of my thoughts and I did not mention even for the sake of the Muslim community we have to compromise the national or the social cohesiveness or integration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister can he provide, can he explain any examples where I am sowing discord and divisiveness.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I actually wonder whether the 	Workers' Party and its leadership are committed to the racial and religious harmony which underpins the security of this country.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Do we want to go back to the politics of race and religion of the 1960s, the politics we wanted to avoid when we left Malaysia?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If we do not want that, why do we let a Member constantly raise these issues to stir the community, to tell them "you are different", to subtly suggest to them "we are not able to address your issues now because the Government won't do it"?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The Minister has not answered my question of an example of where I have caused discord and divisiveness.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: On what Minister mentioned earlier about the issue faced by the community being not easy to resolve, hence, I have been asking persistently and consistently for the Government to address the issue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: That is the point that I have been making since I was elected and I have even started to make this point after the Suara Musyawarah Report was made public, based on that concern voiced in that report, as a basis for my point that I bring up in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If I have not heard the Member, the Member also has not heard me.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Like I mentioned to Mr Faisal Manap, what is worrying me is not so much about whether he intends to sow discord.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The imam did not intend to say anything to hurt the Christians or the Jews.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But the Christians and the Jews, now that it is out in the open, do feel insulted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not only our intention that matters.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is our action and how people interpret it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I met some students in Mecca at Medina very recently and they were unhappy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They were concerned that many people think people who study in Mecca, Medina would have what they call Salafi thinking, not moderate, very extreme.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And they say, "We do not do all these things.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We tell people to do only the right things as a Muslim." But I asked them, "Have you ever checked what people think and what people do after what you said and what you teach them?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Have you ever gone to the ground to check the impact of what you teach them?" As an example, I told them there was a divorce that happened after they got the wife to become very religiously observant.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The wife, because the husband is not so religiously observant, divorced the husband.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And, therefore, as responsible Members of this House, I hope the Member just does not do this as a matter of course because it is a responsibility to do so, even if it is your right to do so, but do this responsibly because we have a context, we have a very precious social fabric to preserve.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I ask the Workers' Party and everybody here, respect that, preserve that.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Because this is something we can leave for our children.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I just like to address one point that was brought up by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: He mentioned that public consultations, including in this Chamber, are not the right places to discuss such matters.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I believe that this is the best platform, an official platform for me as an elected Member of Parliament to bring up the issues.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Indeed, last November, we did mention a very sensitive issue regarding having a Malay or minority to be elected as the Head of State.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I believe that is a sensitive issue that was discussed openly in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, I believe this is the right platform for me to bring up.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: If not here, where else, can I, as an elected Member of Parliament, voice out the concerns of the community?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even when I was not a Member of Parliament, I could talk about this.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I remember in 2002 – please look up the reports – when I was involved in discussions with the Government on a similar issue about uniforms in schools.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I would bet you, a similar situation elsewhere will not happen.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It will continue to make the community upset because nobody will cede what they think is their right.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Policies and initiatives to support working women and women in general have been encouraging and have helped women better manage their multiple roles in the home, at work and in the community.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there is still more that needs to be done.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my speech, I would like to touch on three areas, that of (a) work support for women; (b) shared responsibilities; and (c) financial planning and retirement adequacy, all of which have also been put forward in the PAP Women's Wing position paper published in July last year.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many women, the desire to work or stay at home is shaped by different reasons − personal goals, family responsibilities or the family's economic situation, among others.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The choice is really up to each woman and in consultation with their significant others.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, for women who have decided to stay at home to take care of their children or elderly parents or even family members with special needs, and who, thereafter, decide to return to work, they would need the necessary conditions and provisions to (a) choose between returning to full-time or part-time or flexi-work; (b) have adequate support for their caregiving responsibilities; and (c) learn and re-learn relevant knowledge and skills needed for the work they are returning to.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad to see greater support for women for childcare and elderly caregiving, be it in terms of financial, social or emotional support.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not yet ideal, but we are headed in the right direction.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to see more provisions given to our women to have easier access to learn and re-learn relevant knowledge and skills that are needed for the work they are returning to.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The returnship programme can also include a work placement support and internship programme for our back-to-work women to have enough time to learn about the company they are joining and the work they will be doing.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that our unions also will be able to support such a returnship programme for our back-to-work women.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I would also urge our public sector and private sector employers to make greater provisions for flexi- or part-time work for both mothers and fathers as well.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, flexi-work in the form of allowing several weeks of working from home when family exigencies come up, with no disruption to salaries or performance appraisals, would be ideal.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Allowing working mothers and working fathers to work as a work-team will make it easier for flexi-work to be implemented and taken up, as teammates can cover office duties when a working mother or father needs to do flexi-work and work from home.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such provisions allow for greater flexibility for couples to decide on child or elderly caregiving arrangements depending on the needs of their families and for them to share such responsibilities, which brings me to my next point on shared responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our societal norms and traditions also need to evolve.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, we have to change our perceptions of mothers being the main caregiver for children or the home − for mothers to be the one to cook, clean, wash, teach and take care of our children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fathers have an equally important role to play in caring for our children and in keeping house that extends beyond just putting the children to bed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When our children see their fathers doing housework, lending a hand in changing diapers, or cooking meals at home, we shape our children's perceptions of societal norms and responsibilities and traditions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We broaden their minds and we help them see that both boys and girls have a part to play in keeping the family together and in taking care of the household.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, we also need to change how we perceive elderly caregiving.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Traditionally, we expect daughters or grown-up children who are not married to be the ones to take care of our elderly parents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When this is not possible, we expect others to take care of them − this can be in the form of the Government, nursing homes, or even domestic helpers − to fulfil such responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taking care of our elderly parents is a shared responsibility for everyone in the family − daughters or sons, married or otherwise.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Providing for flexi-work or work-teams or shared work in the workplace, would help us fulfil our caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to greater support from our employers, including from the public sector, in this.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My third point is on financial planning and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More of our women are now working − whether full-time, part-time or doing freelancing work to supplement the family income.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this point, Mdm Speaker, please allow me to continue in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   More and more of our women are now working and are able to provide for the family.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Compared to our grandparents' time, women today are more highly educated, possess 21st century competencies and skills and have more opportunities to work, to acquire knowledge and global experience and also to pursue their interests further.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the decision to be a homemaker is a personal one, I am, nonetheless, concerned about the ability of our women to, firstly, plan for their long-term financial needs and capacity; and, secondly, ensure their retirement adequacy in old age.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I respect the decision of Malay women when they want to be full-time homemakers or to work part-time while their primary responsibility is raising children and taking care of the household.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But at the same time, I do hope our women will plan more carefully for their long-term financial needs and capacity.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, they should plan to save from a young age for their children's education − whether through a savings account in the bank or through an education insurance scheme for their children − as well as engage in financial planning for themselves.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our women should have personal savings for their own needs, too.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have no family support, alone and helpless, and are dependent on public sympathy and compassion.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel heartbroken whenever I meet them and I hope I will never see such a situation becoming widespread among our Malay women.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With due respect to our men, I urge and make this appeal to our women that they should not be too dependent on their husbands financially and for retirement adequacy in old age.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Regardless of whether our women choose to be full-time homemakers or to work part-time or work full-time, I hope they have clear plans that ensure their own financial independence and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this point, Mdm Speaker, I would like to close my speech in English.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Over the years, more provisions and support have been given to help women manage our multiple roles and responsibilities − in the family, at work and in the community.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While such provisions and support have been encouraging, certainly, more can still be done to ensure that our women can continue to be the best daughters, best wives, best mothers, best employees, best leaders and important members of our community for now and the future.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, we can ask for changes to be made.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But sometimes, we need to make those changes ourselves.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has been said, "There is no force more powerful than a woman determined to rise".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, rise, mothers, daughters, sisters and let us be the change we want to see in our community and in the world.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With grandma doing menial jobs to support her many children, mom having had some form of education and working in an SME or a factory, my current generation with greater access to education options and working in jobs that we desire and, finally, our children, having the possibility to be what they want to be and living lives that are meaningful and fulfilling.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At this point, given the progress that women have made in Singapore, what more can be done to ensure that we, the mothers, sisters and daughters of Singapore, can be the best that we can be and, in so doing, give the best to those around us?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We aspire for equal opportunity – the opportunity to be recognised fairly for the work that we do, the opportunity to rise up in a corporate or in the community for the efforts that we put in.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the increasing numbers of women as employees and as consumers, companies may be missing an important perspective on their products and services as well as the management of their company, by not tapping on the perspectives that women bring.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Diversity Action Committee (DAC) has done important work in this area.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With their database of suitable women candidates for board positions and a knowledge of the capability requirements to become a board director, corporates facing difficulties identifying suitable women candidates for board positions could interface more with DAC.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) and Trade Associations, with their network of employers, can also play an active role by putting these employers in touch with DAC.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A little step every way can help us narrow this yawning gap in women in corporate leadership.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women also aspire to positions in community leadership.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With increasing social spending from the Government on healthcare and childcare needs and a greater call for a whole-of-society approach to dealing with our society's needs, perhaps there can be more targeted recruitment, training and retention activities aimed at women volunteers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women volunteers can bring in very different strengths and capabilities in community work and address the needs of special groups in the community.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At different junctures of our lives, women may have to make decisions to balance competing needs of their careers and their families.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we were to take a life-cycle approach to the decisions that women have to make, it may be easier to identify the pressure points that women face.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The work of Young Women's Leadership Connection (YWLC) is thus important as its network of women mentors can help support young women leaders in their journey to fulfil their aspirations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we further support the work of YWLC?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The next juncture where women may face disruptions in their careers could be due to childbearing or the need to care for the elderly in the family.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we go a step further and identify the industries that show the highest drop-out rate for women and tailor the engagement for these women to encourage them to stay in the workforce?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Flexible work arrangements are one way to encourage people to stay in the workforce who might otherwise have dropped out.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just as there are industry transformation maps for technology, there can be industry transformation maps for HR practices.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I hope that the tripartite partners can work together to identify which industries and which areas of work can be most easily flexi-ed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can there be more granular work arrangements so that flexi-work, flexi-place and flexi-load can truly be implementable?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Jobs can be shared and, correspondingly, wages can be apportioned.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With greater deliberation, we can try to customise work arrangements to bring in workers who otherwise might not be able to participate in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, alleviating stress points around childcare can also help women and, in so doing, release constraints that potentially impede them from making optimal choices in their careers and family life.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, childcare options in estates with many young families have been a perennial bugbear.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It would be helpful if MOE can consider setting up childcare centres, as young parents need full-day childcare facilities to take care of their toddlers while they are at work.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, the opening hours till 7.00 pm for most childcare operators create a huge stress point for young parents who are not able to reach the school on time to pick up their children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Most working adults I know finish work after 6.00 pm.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A little step of the way can go a long way towards helping our women.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are responsible and stand by the choices we make in our lives.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But do ensure that equal opportunities are made available to us.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Help us make the choices we make easier as we are trying our best to be a good wife, a good mother and a useful citizen.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By being the best that we can be, we can give our best to you.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   At different junctures of our lives, women may have to make decisions to balance the competing needs of their careers and their families.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The work of Young Women's Leadership Connection is thus very important.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The next juncture women may face could be due to childbearing or the need to care for the elderly in the family.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we all work together to see which industries and which areas of work can be most easily flexi-ed?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, alleviating stress points around childcare is also important for women.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A little step forward can go a long way towards helping our women.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Please help her by ensuring that equal opportunities are made available to her.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Help her make the choices easier as she is trying her best to be a good wife, a good mother and a useful citizen.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Your understanding will be rewarded by her giving her best to you.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They manage an amazing career, sew their own buttons, make home-cooked meals, tutor their brilliant children and somehow, still manage to look Instagram-worthy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And yes, these amazing unicorns apparently exist and I do not know how they do it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: On weekdays, I still struggle to leave office on time to be at home for my child.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And on weekends or weeknights, I have unfinished business to clear, like writing this speech, for instance.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot do anything without my husband and domestic helper playing tag-team with me.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The year that my father fell ill and my kid was just born was also the first year that I took up the Nominated Member of Parliament position, on top of all my other work.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A few weeks ago, after Budget season, I received an online message from a woman whom I have never met.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She was not asking for any answers and she was not requesting for any favours.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She was just hoping for someone to feel her present struggle and care for her future story.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She wrote, "I am a mother to four boys, married to a civil servant, but you have no idea how hard life has been for us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We keep on trying and striving and doing our best to survive, not for ourselves, but for our boys.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I wake up every day at 4.30 am in the morning to cook because my children cannot eat the food from school, and I have been packing their lunches for more than 10 years.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I rush to cook, clean and get my kids ready for school.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We live far away, and my husband sends them to school each morning, but I will rush to my office to work.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Then, I will fetch my kids home by bus.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I cook lunch and sit down with my kids for revision, I check their homework.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am not well-educated, so I also have to engage tutors for the boys.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My business does not earn very much, but I do it anyway just for the kids, to pay for tuition fees, to help my husband out.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And yes, the story is long and boring and tiring, but that is how I feel, too.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, I will cry myself to sleep, and feel that I have failed as a mum who cannot provide enough for her children and as an only daughter who cannot provide enough for her own mother.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Bills and more bills to pay, problems after problems.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It gets very frustrating and I wish someone could listen to what I have to say and understand my plight, but sadly no one is there.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And we only have our family, just us." I wanted to bring her voice in this House so that we can get a sense of what at least one real woman on the ground might be thinking as she listens to us discuss in theory how to affirm every woman's contributions and support her aspirations.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Her story is not representative of every Singapore woman's story, but I believe it does have enough threads within to bind it to a wider tapestry of even tougher tales out there.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For many women, it is difficult to aspire about a faraway future, where the demands of the present feel so overwhelming.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Planning for the future is a luxury only those of us who have the privilege of time and mental bandwidth can afford.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And yes, a woman who has cash to spare in her household budget can have the option of purchasing the spare time and mental bandwidth she needs in the present to improve her future prospects.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She can hire a domestic worker to clean the house and cook the meals.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She can pay for laundry to be pressed and groceries to be delivered.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She can hire school buses to do the fetching and tutors to do the revising.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She can engage the best live-in nurses for her parents and all-day preschools for her kids.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And she can pay for financial planners to strategise the growth of her savings and investments.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, yes, theoretically, a woman can outsource all the jobs in her extensive portfolio of home-based work to an army of many to do, but many women do not.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many women take on either the full or partial portfolio of caregiving work onto themselves.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And for some women, it is a deliberate and happy choice.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They may have the wealth to pay for external help and they are personally convicted that some types of domestic work, particularly caregiving for their ageing parents or young children, are too sacred to be outsourced to strangers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They derive great personal satisfaction from being a full-time worker at home, rather than a full-time worker in the office.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And they may take a financial hit for their choice, but they have enough financial reserves and social support to feel at peace about their future.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They may also have done their math and compared the income they would derive from working versus the cost they would pay for external help, and then they sacrifice the job they enjoy to be a caregiver because it is just the more affordable option.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They do want to care for their loved ones and they do so either on a full-time or part-time basis, but they are also clear that they want to go back to office work someday, either because they have personal goals to fulfil or because they know they just need the income.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My focus today is on how we can better support the aspirations in future of this second group of women.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Statistically, women tend to shoulder a significantly larger portion of the burden of unpaid invisible caregiving work, much more so than men.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In 2014, it was 70,060 women who left, compared to 3,564 men.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The number of women who leave the visible paid labour force to enter the invisible and unpaid labour force of domestic caregiving is a big deal because, firstly, the labour is not free.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Presently, we have many older women today, widows or single unmarried women who currently face financial insecurity because they sacrificed their lifetime earnings and savings to care for dependants at the peak of their working years.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Kanwaljit Soin observed in a 2012 interview with the Council for Third Age (C3A) that, usually, because women live longer than men, the women will be looking after her husband through his last illness, spending most of their savings on him.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: After he dies, she is without a spouse, with little material resources left and there are about five times as many widows than widowers in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In a tight labour market like ours, especially given our low birth rates, we do have to increase our female labour participation rate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But if we want more of our women to stay in the labour force or re-enter it after their time of caregiving, we must provide better systemic support for their work of caregiving.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My first request is on behalf of the financial future of full-time home-based caregivers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A 2015/2016 CPF Advisory Panel Recommendations Report expressed worry about the financial vulnerability of our female caregivers who leave the workforce and are completely reliant on their husband's CPF payouts for their retirement.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Should these caregivers outlive their husbands, they will have no sustained income.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Member of Parliament Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has suggested having a system of automatic transfers with an opt-out option from an income-earning spouse to a non-income earning caregiver spouse's account under the Retirement Sum Topping-Up Scheme.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If voluntary transfers do not climb significantly, then I think we have to consider this intrusive option.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I also wonder if we can encourage income-earning spouses, children, relatives or even friends to contribute to some kind of Caregiver Development Account.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It allows the community to practically honour the work of the caregivers that they love as well as encourage the caregivers to take care of their own well-being and development.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It could be something like how the Government currently encourages parents to save for their child's future through the Child Development Account.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The state can offer a cap of one-for-one matching grant over a fixed time period and the money can similarly only be taken out by the caregiver for a select range of self-care or self-development activities, to ensure that claimants are true caregivers rather than opportunists.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Claimants should be required to identify the range of activities of daily living that they do so on behalf of a care recipient.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This initiative could also be limited only to claimants or care recipients who do not employ foreign domestic workers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My second request is on behalf of the career aspirations of lower income mothers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is really difficult to go on job searches or training workshops without first getting access to alternative caregiving help.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I echo Member of Parliament Cheryl Chan's call to relook the chicken-and-egg situation some of these mothers are caught in where they need to be employed before receiving state subsidies for childcare.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We could explore granting jobseekers from lower income households a limited number of months of childcare subsidies upon application.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: After that, they can show periodic proof that they are on a genuine job search by showing evidence of registration with job-matching agencies like e2i or job applications with potential employers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Such transitional support will be a valuable boost to their morale and motivate the search for stable work within the timeframe of the given childcare subsidies.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My third request is a long-term and more drastic one.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate Minister of State Lam Pin Min's sharing yesterday of the Ministry's efforts to improve access to caregiving and respite services but still I believe that as long as we leave caregiving as a problem primarily for individual families to resolve, then we will continue to see individual women become the solution by leaving paid employment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A national system of caregiving will not only allow women providing unpaid care at home to return to the workforce with more confidence, it will also be most impactful on the fortunes of the low-income and sandwich-class families who need these resources most.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not bring this up lightly because I know it is an extremely costly, complex and controversial venture and the staffing cost alone will be huge.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I imagine such a system cannot be supported purely by tax dollar-paid professionals alone but by an army of unpaid volunteers as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: At the risk of laying yet another burden of care on us women, there is a controversial solution I have heard before which I believe we will have to debate about in due course.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The possibilities for societal impact could be stunning and so will the personal cost.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Young women will have to give up their time and opportunity and freedom but this is the very same price we have asked our young men to pay all these years for military conscription.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Universal female conscription may not be a popular idea for now but, in stark contrast, the idea that National Service is noble work and an excellent character-building opportunity for fathers, husbands, boyfriends or sons is.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Given that, our men have sacrificed so much over the first 50 years to serve and defend our country.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It only seems fair for us women to also keep an open mind and a willing heart for the next 50 years to answer the call to serve and defend the communities we love, should that request ever be made of us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know if female community-based conscription will ever be a reality but I do know that, if it ever does come to pass, I will be very glad to have my own daughter serve the nation that way.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If I am not too old by then and this country will still have me, I will be equally glad to serve alongside.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I want to close my speech by bringing us back to that first woman's story.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It was she who inspired me to speak on this Motion because reading her message, while I felt for her sorrows, I also felt great admiration for her strengths.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Women like her wrote the book on hard work and resilience.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: No matter how hopeless things feel, how tired they are, how many tears they have shed, they know how to get up, wipe the mess and soldier on like the warriors that they are.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She is struggling but she is not giving up − not yet.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many women like her are already fighting for their aspirations and their families' futures.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They just want to know whether we are in our own trenches fighting for them, too, because just knowing that we are together in this fight makes their fight feel a little easier.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that many of us from both sides of the House do share the hope to help our women.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We and the rest of this nation can be that larger family beyond their own that they need.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There are very real barriers of time, bandwidth, privilege and bureaucracy that stand in their way that are very difficult for them to overcome by themselves.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Let us give our fighting women a fighting chance at their dreams of the future by meeting them halfway and breaking down those walls for them a brick at a time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both my grandmothers were homemakers and, in their generation, most of their female counterparts would similarly be at home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my maternal grandmother's case, she came to Singapore from India in order to be educated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, after Primary 1, World War II broke out and her education was stopped.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: After the war, her guardian told her that, as a woman, it was not good to be too educated because it would be difficult to get married and that was the end of her education.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, post-Independence Singapore was a very different place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The PAP Government at that time governed on the premise that men and women should have equal opportunities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both boys and girls had to have Primary education and school fees were nominal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My parents' generation saw the benefit of these changes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My mother and all the aunts had full education, unlike their own mothers, and joined the workforce after their education.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, my maternal grandmother, whose own education was cut short, did the reverse with her daughters and would chase them out of the kitchen when they tried to help, telling them they should study instead.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These dramatic changes took place in a single generation since Singapore's Independence and have changed Singapore life completely.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Women have become economically empowered and educated, which gives them a degree of independence the previous generations never had.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even with these dramatic changes, it gave me some pride actually to read the Women's Wing paper on "Singapore's future − women's perspectives and aspirations".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That was what inspired me to come forward and speak for this Motion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Because while we have made great strides to create equality, educational opportunities, there is, I think, still more that can be done.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was with some pride that I read the Women's Wing paper where it started out by saying, "Although Singapore enjoys high female labour force participation, women saw their social impact, not only through contributions at the workplace but also through performing multiple roles in the family, as daughters, sisters, wives and mothers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Though motivated primarily by intrinsic satisfaction, societal recognition of their familial and societal contributions remains important".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My reading of the paper is that women's aspirations were really to try and do it all, far greater aspirations that I think many men would have.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They want to be the ideal person at home; they also want to be the ideal person at work and have opportunities there; these are difficult to do.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are many things in this paper which I would recommend everyone to read because, from beginning to end, it covers a whole range of areas from leadership and societal impact, employment, entrepreneurship, family and caregiving, financial well-being and the concerns women have towards the end of their life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I will focus on, perhaps, the two more optimistic areas, the happier ones.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What I will call empowering women for the women who really want to try to have it all.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What the crux of this boils down to is how women can get help when they come to the difficult part of their life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This tends to happen in their 30s because that is when female workforce participation drops relative to male workforce participation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is largely attributed to playing greater roles in the family and at home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many women do not see this as an imposition but this is a role that they seek to take up on their own.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of the suggestions in the Women's Wing paper are actually very thoughtful to meet this need.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would just highlight a few of those that I think are particularly useful.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first, of course, is flexible work, which I think has been bandied about quite often in this debate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes simple things: creating opportunities for women to work from home, telecommuting and more flexible hours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But, of course, at a theoretical level, this is very easy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To implement it is not always as easy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This new paper is more nuanced and recognises that having a legislation to that effect may actually cause problems or may cause fears for employers employing women.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is important because it has to be a nuanced approach that all parties, employers included, must buy into and agree with.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, it is my hope that employers will recognise that this is in the long-term interest of their business as well because they keep talented people in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I should also add that flexible work should be open to both genders, both men and women.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In many ways, this will also encourage more men to take up roles at home, if they know that such flexible work arrangements are available for all parties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second set of areas relate to caregiving facilities that are made available and the network of support that is available for women.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Flexible work is certainly an aspiration and one which I think we can start working on a short measure through a tripartite workgroup.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But in the meantime, just as I think many speakers have acknowledged, part of the reason women drop out of the workforce is because they take on the caregiving role.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the suggestions in the paper is also to rethink how childcare and eldercare facilities are designed and situated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The key being that these should be situated in places that are easy for women and actually men as well to drop off children, seniors if necessary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These caregiving places can also not only surely be near where people stay but also near where people work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The next is to develop a network of caregivers or what some other people might have called social capital.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This can be done with an online directory created to help match supply and demand.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is a very simple solution but it involves creating awareness of where these caregivers are, whether it is in the neighbourhood, whether it is outside, whether it is near the workplace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As long as credentials of these people are available and somewhat regulated, this could be another alternative for caregiving.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, if people are accessed according to their contributions, rather than the amount of time they spend at work, that could lead to fairer appraisal systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Also, one of our aspirations is to make sure that women are able to stay at work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is also important to give back-to-work support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If people take some time out of the workforce, they should be given as much opportunity as possible to come back.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There has been an extensive study that diversity, in fact, adds to the value of companies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There was a McKenzie study in 2015, which I believe the paper cited.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But the point is this, this is a correlation, it is not really causation but there seems to be strong evidence that diversity creates more perspectives on the board, more viewpoints and more reach for companies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But diversity is sometimes not always easy to achieve because people tend to get onto boards together with others they are more comfortable with and, sometimes, if you take someone who is different from you, either gender or ethnicity, it may be a little unnatural at first.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That is why sometimes having some kind of quotas may be helpful.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think that may be a little bit unnatural at first but I think that it is something that will, in the long term, be in the best interests of all companies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As this is also the Tamil Language Festival, let me just end with a little bit of wisdom in Tamil.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   She will make butter out of bought buttermilk and pay for her eldest son's wedding.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In English): This is a proverb, which basically says, a mother will make butter from butter milk, which is the alternative to yoghurt and, with that, pay for the wedding of a son.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, this is from a different era but the idea of the proverb is the ingenuity of women.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And even in that day and age, where there was something important to be done, the women would be able to do the impossible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My own view is, given the amenities of today, they would probably be able to outshine us and do even more impossible things.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am excited and encouraged by the initiative of the PAP Women's Wing to spearhead a project centred upon the empowerment of women to their fullest potential.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While inroads and improvements in this area are evident, building awareness and continued engagement must persist in order to enable our women to aspire without real or perceived inhibitions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Japan, a mature democracy like Singapore, has a target of women occupying 30% of the Japanese Parliament by 2020 pursuant to their White Paper on Gender Equality 2011.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The figure of 30% is not a figure without any basis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to the Diversity Action Committee which was established by MSF, it is increasingly common for women to be leaders in the boardroom, in addition to being a mother, wife and daughter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the private sector recognises that women are capable enough to take on onerous responsibilities, I believe we should also look out for suitable candidates and nurture them to take on portfolios in the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is not to say the private sector is highly exemplary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to the same Committee, due to the perceived shortage of qualified women and preferences for qualified directors who are men, progress is hamstrung.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Committee further observed that Singapore lags behind the UK, Australia, Hong Kong and Malaysia in terms of female representation on boards of directors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, Singapore's number of qualified women should be similar to these countries, given our enviable quality of education coupled with high economic activities for all to participate in and prove their worth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, I would like to indicate my support for the 2020 target announced by Minister Grace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, we can and we have, to have to ensure that at least 20% of female directors on boards by 2020.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Boardroom representation is not the only issue of concern.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A few weeks ago, NUS released a study showing that female executive directors of Singapore Exchange-listed companies earned just 56.1% of what their male counterparts earned.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I sincerely hope that businesses will examine their remuneration policies and structures, and put forward new remuneration frameworks that better reflect the value women bring to the economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I strongly encourage businesses and not-for-profit entities, both big and small, to be on the look-out for capable women and provide them with opportunities to prove that they are just as good as, if not better than, their male counterparts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A noteworthy corporate entity is one of Singapore's biggest law firms, WongPartnership, where 43% of the executive committee is made up of women.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Rachel Eng, joint Managing Partner of WongPartnership said, "Our firm did not set a target to achieve gender diversity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, by creating a culture that recognises and accepts that our talents, including female talents, may need special support during certain periods of their lives, we were able to create a conducive culture for our talents to thrive." I hope that more corporate entities will create conducive cultures that recognise and accept all talents, regardless of their gender.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Besides creating a conducive culture at work, I believe the culture set at home and societal mindset must be reworked, too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is possible that unequal distribution of care plays a major role in explaining the disparity in representation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In studying the Age-Sex Specific Resident Labour Force Participation Rate, Singapore does not have the "M" curve of other developed economies, where women leave the workforce when children are young but return in significant numbers later in life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, it is just a decline with time.
